#3315. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3314. Zosia Mamet Says ‘Girls’ Revival Was “In Talks For A Very Long Time”: “I Kind Of Gave Up”

Nearly 10 years after last playing Shoshanna Shapiro, Zosia Mamet was beginning to think a Girls revival wasn’t in the cards.

The actress, who starred in the Lena Dunham-created HBO comedy, admitted that she wasn’t sure the recently announced revival wouldn’t happen after the five-episode project had been in development “for a very long time.”

“I mean, it’s been in talks for a very long time,” she explained to Entertainment Tonight. “But I kind of gave up because we’ve been talking about it for so long, and I don’t trust anything until I’m actually on set.”

Mamet added, “Once they officially made an offer, it kind of came together pretty fast. So, I didn’t have to keep a secret for too long, which is good, because I’m not a good secret keeper.” Watch on Deadline

Last month, series creator and star Dunham was joined by Mamet and co-stars Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke and Andrew Rannells for a video announcing the HBO Original revival, which begins production in 2027.

Zosia Mamet thinks the internet’s theories about Shoshanna’s storyline in the 'Girls' revival may be a little too accurate. 😭 pic.twitter.com/b9vL1Ljvg4

Dunham created and starred in Girls as millennial writer Hannah Horvath, navigating her 20s in New York City. The show ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017.

#3311. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

AI slop is a small problem for Wikipedia. The bigger problem is very biased editing on anything with even minimal political implication. And that's a human problem, not AI.

#3309. Sports TV Schedule Could Be Tackled For Loss In Aftermath Of FAA’s Nationwide Flight Halt

College football’s Saturday TV slate appears likely to take a hit from the FAA‘s decision Friday to impose a ground halt on all U.S. airline traffic, which in turn could disrupt many network sports schedules on a busy weekend.

The agency late Friday began allowing flights to depart after more than four hours in a stoppage that saw more than 800 flights diverted and more than 10,000 overall impacted by the first such incident since 9/11. The FAA and the Department of Transportation blamed a “communication issue” that forced the shutdown “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

In the world of college football, ABC, CBS, NBC, ESPN, Fox and The CW are among networks facing possible game postponements. Media outlets spent the day determining whether teams had either already made it to their game sites, were in the air at the time of the stoppage or had not left their home airports before the shutdown. Watch on Deadline

Some schools quickly took alternate means of transportation, with the University of Alabama driving to Nashville for its game against Vanderbilt, while Purdue is taking a bus to Iowa State as is Auburn to Mississippi State, according to the Associated Press. USC arrived ahead of the ban for its game at Indiana, while Boston College made it to South Bend, IN for its game with Notre Dame.

The University of Texas, due to travel to play LSU in one of the day’s marquee games, were among several teams forced to deplane before takeoff, like the University of Washington before their trip to Michigan State.

Statement from the Southeastern Conference on FAA nationwide ground stop: pic.twitter.com/IIU4TnwMVJ

Two Friday night games involving ranked teams will have complications for the visitors returning home, with Illinois at UCLA and Houston at Colorado.

The NBA is also likely to see some shifting of games, but its Saturday slate is fairly low-wattage compared with Friday night’s Prime Video doubleheader. One story that percolated today: the Brooklyn Nets got stuck on the tarmac in New Orleans trying to get to Memphis to play the Grizzlies on Saturday.

The top draw in TV sports, the NFL, seems to have caught a break with the schedule. New England and Detroit are set to play in Germany on Sunday morning, but teams typically travel well in advance of international games in order to adjust to the time difference, meaning they were onsite when the FAA order was given. Depending on the length of the shutdown, there could be a question about the return flights to the U.S.

Across the rest of the NFL’s Sunday slate, most games are due to be played by teams within 500 miles of each other, meaning a Saturday bus trip wouldn’t be out of the question. Exceptions include the San Francisco 49ers playing at the Dallas Cowboys; the Seattle Seahawks at the Las Vegas Raiders; and the Miami Dolphins at the Indianapolis Colts.

In soccer, the U.S. Men’s National Team and Haiti both made it to Miami ahead of their CONCACAF Nation’s League game Saturday. It airs live at 4:30 p.m. ET on TBS, truTV, HBO Max, Universo and Peacock.

Patrick Hipes contributed to this report.

#3308. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3307. Apple to investigate accident that killed three workers at iPhone parts factory in India

Reuters reports that three contract workers died after inhaling gas during an inspection at a Tata Electronics factory that produces iPhone components in India. Here are the details.

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple’s supply chain in India relies heavily on Tata, which manufactures iPhone components and accounts for a significant share of the country’s iPhone assembly operations.

Since Apple began diversifying its manufacturing operations away from China, India has emerged as a major production hub, with roughly a quarter of the world’s iPhones now manufactured in the country.

Earlier this year, Apple found itself linked to an environmental controversy in India, after the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board investigated allegations that wastewater from a Tata facility had contaminated nearby farmland water.

A few weeks later, however, Tata said the regulator had dropped further action against the facility after the company addressed the concerns raised.

At the time, Tata said it had ordered separate testing related to the facility and that the results supported its position that the plant was operating within the rules.

However, the matter was apparently not fully resolved, as just three days later, Reuters reported that local health officials were still investigating complaints from nearby farmers.

And while there had been no major developments reported about the wastewater investigation since then, Reuters reported today that three contract workers died in an accident at the same Tata facility.

The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment ​plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility, which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, ​district official Dinesh Kumar said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

The report added that Tata and Tamil Nadu authorities are also investigating the fatal accident, and noted that “production was not affected as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week.”

#3306. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3305. DC Studios To-Do List: Here’s What Incoming Boss Jeremy Latcham Will Sort Through From The Gunn-Safran Era

The news earlier this week of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s exit from DC shook the town like Suicide Squad‘s Starro stomping down Melrose Avenue. Now it’s up to incoming former Marvel executive and Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves producer Jeremy Latcham to sort through the groundwork that was laid before by the duo.

You can check out the list of lingering and active DC projects below.

Note, Latcham starts the job December 1, and we understand that no mandates have been given to him by Skydance co-CEO David Ellison in regards to what’s prioritized among those projects in development.

Gunn and Safran’s “Gods and Monsters” vision, which was first unveiled in January 2023, was realized at 40%, with movies Superman and Supergirl made along with TV series Lanterns and Creature Commandos. Having seen the ills in the Marvel Cinematic Universe owing to its overindulgence in the Disney+ era with features being fast-tracked and storylines between series and movies mish-moshed, Gunn was adamant about not rushing projects through development — or worse, going into production on a movie that was missing a third act. If a project wasn’t ready, it wasn’t ready, which is why we saw some of the early pitches promised — i.e., Paradise Lost and Booster Gold series, and the antihero team The Authority feature — ultimately stall. Watch on Deadline

James Mangold was circling Swamp Thing at one point a few years ago, but the five-time Oscar-nominated filmmaker is currently making his Paramount+ series Copland a priority. Not to mention he’s also working on a motocross heist screenplay that reteams him with his A Complete Unknown star Timothée Chalamet for the film studio.

Another thing Gunn and Safran wanted to correct in Warners’ DC-verse were the dueling TV and film mythologies for superheroes. Quite often a superhero’s storyline on TV was different on the big screen, or worse, competed against each other. Case in point: the CW series of Flash ended in May 2023, three weeks before the Ezra Miller-fronted movie hit theaters and bombed with $271.4 million worldwide off a $200M production cost before P&A (the star’s tabloid headlines at the time didn’t help the movie either). The Gunn and Safran DC universe would see their characters having direct lines through live-action film and TV. Above all, Gunn’s m.o. was to bring zhuzh to a franchise that had grown stale after Christopher Nolan’s Dark Knight series.

It will be interesting to see whether Latcham remains as strict as Gunn and Safran were on development.

In the run-up to the Paramount-Warner Bros merger, Gunn and Safran didn’t greenlight any live-action feature films beyond what was currently in production, so only The Batman Part II, Man of Tomorrow and The Dynamic Duo. Gunn has teased he’s got a screenplay he’s penning in the DC-verse post-Man of Tomorrow, but that greenlight will be up to Team Latcham (he worked with Gunn during Guardians of the Galaxy).

A bulk of what Gunn and Safran leave behind to DC’s new owners are animated TV series. Given the nature of animation production, many of these projects are already in the works even though many don’t have a streaming or network home, or even a renewal.

The new Warner Bros under Skydance co-CEOs Ellison and Ynon Kreiz remains strictly about keeping everything in the black. In a recent earnings call, the two were vocal about the bleeding that was going on in the YTD Warner Bros feature slate. There’s no room for box office kryptonite ala this past summer’s blunder Supergirl (production cost $186M, global box office $126.4M), arguably the only big miss during the Gunn and Safran administration (versus the previous Walter Hamada-run era that yielded The Flash, Shazam: Fury of the Gods and Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom).

Above all, the new Paramount administration, which declined comment for this story, is conscious about not repeating history, meaning cancelling a near-completed project to the greater upset of the town (remember how David Zaslav swatted Batgirl in August 2022? That was all before Gunn and Safran arrived on the scene).

Below is the list of projects remaining at DC.

Man of Tomorrow (dir. James Gunn) – The Superman sequel starring David Corenswet, Rachel Brosnahan and Nicholas Hoult is in post-production and set for release on July 9, 2027. Buzz is that Lanterns segues into this Superman. Gunn took to Threads to respond to rumors that Skydance is making edits to the film. “No one from Skydance has even seen the movie – the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false,” exclaimed the MCU and DCU filmmaker.

The Batman Part II (dir. Matt Reeves). After Reeves stepped away for personal reasons, Steven Soderbergh is finishing the sequel to 2022’s $772M-grossing Robert Pattinson movie in London for a February 18, 2028 theatrical release.

Dynamic Duo (dir Arthur Mintz) – The origin story of the Robins is a co-production with Warner Bros Pictures Animation, 6th and Idaho and New Orleans animation studio Swaybox. The latter is known for their “momo animation,” which is a cross between CGI animation, stop-motion practical elements and live-action real-time performance. Pic will hit theaters on September 22, 2028.

Bat-Fam – Season 1 premiered in November 2025, with the second half of the season still to air on the Prime Video series showrun by Mike Roth. Batman, Alfred and young Damian Wayne — having taken on the mantle of “Little Batman” — welcome a few new residents to Wayne Manor. Joining the family dinner table is Alicia Pennyworth, Alfred’s free-spirited grandniece; Claire, a recently reformed Super-Villain; Ra’s al Ghul, Damian’s adoring “Pap Pap” who also happens to be Batman’s longtime nemesis; and Man-Bat, who takes up residence in the belfry. Oh! And let’s not forget Selina, the beloved family cat. This close-knit family of misfits navigate the fun and frustrations of ordinary life while protecting the streets of Gotham City.

Batman Caped Crusader – The Prime Video series has clocked two seasons and is awaiting renewal. Executive producers/showrunners are James Tucker and Geoffrey Thorne. EPs are Bruce Timm, James Abrams and Matt Reeves.

Batman: Knightfall – The home entertainment animated feature from director Jeff Wamester and producer Jim Krieg. Part 1 was released in August, Part 2 is happening in December and Part 3 is coming in 2027. This movie event brings to life one of the most iconic sagas in Batman comics history.

The People vs Gorilla Grood – The HBO half hour comedy series, a spinoff of Gunn’s Superman, centers around Skyler Gisondo’s Jimmy Olsen and Jimmy Tatro’s titular ape. It is in post-production with no airdate yet. A super-intelligent ape is convicted of murdering his father, the King of Gorilla City. In an eight-part “true” crime docuseries, the Daily Planet’s Olsen reopens the case, investigating whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongly convicted in one of Metropolis’ most famous murder trials. Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault are showrunners, writers and EPs.

Creature Commandos Season 2 – The James Gunn-created series is in production for a second season; Gunn previously mentioned that an airdate was being eyed for the latter part of 2027. The series follows incarcerated monsters who are recruited for missions deemed too dangerous for humans. Characters joining in Season 2 are Khalis the Mummy, King Shark and Nosferata. Dean Lorey is the showrunner and EP.

DC Super Powers – In production, with a network and streaming home TBD. Matt Beans is the showrunner. At the Alliance School for Heroes, new students Lightning, Flash, Plastic Man, Aquagirl, Green Lantern and Terra level up their powers under the supervision of Principal Martian Manhunter in the hopes of one day graduating and becoming the next generation of Earth’s defenders.

Get Jiro – Season 1 is currently airing on Adult Swim, while Season 2 awaits a greenlight. EPs are showrunners Jordan Blum, Alessandro Tanaka and Brian Gatewood. Starring Brian Tee (Chicago Med), Get Jiro transports viewers to a post-apocalyptic, near-future Los Angeles where culinary culture reigns supreme and the world’s most powerful figures are chefs. In this society where food is both currency and a demarcation of class, the mysterious sushi chef Jiro (Tee) sets out on a quest for vengeance.

Joker: Laugh Riot – The anime Joker series from director Yasuhuro Aoki (ChaO) is in its early days of production, has been greenlit to series and will be taken to market. When Batman is murdered, the Joker launches a ruthless crusade through Gotham’s underworld to find the killer who took away his greatest adversary. But as his violent quest for answers pushes him closer towards vigilante than villain, Joker is forced to confront the truth that without Batman, he doesn’t know who he is.

Mister Miracle – Tom King, who wrote the Mister Miracle comics with Mitch Gerads, is showrunning and EPing this animated series that follows the “odyssey” of Scott Free aka Mister Miracle. Announced at Annecy 2025, the blurb for this series reads: No prison can hold him. No trap can contain him. He is Scott Free, the worldwide celebrity sensation known as Mister Miracle, and he is the greatest escape artist who ever lived. But can he pull off the ultimate trick – and escape death itself? Something goes horribly wrong with the perfect life that Scott and his warrior wife Big Barda have built for themselves on Earth.” The series is in production but hasn’t been sold to a platform yet. It will be taken to market.

My Adventures with Green Lantern – Jake Wyatt, who is also the EP on My Adventures with Superman, is the showrunner for the 10-episode animated series, which follows Jessica Cruz (Moana‘s Auliʻi Cravalho), who made her first appearance in the third season of My Adventures with Superman. She’s a student at Hal Jordan Memorial High. Things get even worse when more debris from the Lanterns’ ancient space war arrives – along with their alien foes. To protect the Earth, Jess will have to overcome her fears, anxieties and your typical teenage drama to lead a new Lantern Corp against a terrifying foe. Other Green Lantern characters in the show include Kyle Rayner and Kilowog. In production but not not sold to a platform a yet.

My Adventures With Superman – This hasn’t been picked up for a fourth season but just finished Season 3 on Adult Swim. Jake Wyatt is EP/showrunner. It’s the animated version of the Superman story with Superman falling in love with Lois Lane and her taking Jimmy Olsen under her wing.

Starfire – Josie Campbell, a writer on My Adventures with Superman, is leading the animated series project for DC Studios and Warner Bros. Animation. The series followed the beloved Teen Titans superhero’s origins when she discovers an ancient spacecraft on her home planet and ventures out to the deepest places of the DC universe. In production but not sold to a platform yet.

Teen Titans Go! – The longest-running DC animated series, with Season 9 currently airing on Cartoon Network and approaching its 500th episode. Luke Cormican is the showrunner.

Batman: Brave and the Bold – The feature project was first announced in 2023 when Gunn and Safran unveiled their “Gods and Monsters” slate with Flash director Andy Muschietti attached to direct. Christina Hodson did a draft of the script. There’s been no movement on this for quite some time however and it’s current slate is unclear. Muschietti has been busy on Season 2 of HBO’s IT: Welcome to Derry. The comic revolves around Batman and his son, Damien Wayne, as Robin “who is a little son of a bitch,” exclaimed Gunn back in 2023. “Assassin, murderer who Batman takes on, who is Batman’s actual son that he doesn’t know exists for the first 8-10 years of his life… it’s a strange father-and-son story about the two of them and based on Grant Morrison’s run of The Batman.” The dilemma with this project from the start is that it’s a complete reboot of Batman, and with the success of Reeves’ The Batman and its upcoming sequel, it’s unclear how two Batman live-action feature franchises could ever exist.

Savage Hunters – Aka the Bane and Deathstroke movie. Greg Mottola was attached to direct off a screenplay by Matthew Orton.

Teen Titans – At lst report, Supergirl scribe Ana Nogueira was taking a stab at it.

Wonder Woman – Ana Nogueira was also writing the first draft of this.

Absolute Batman – From EP Scott Snyder, the series will reinvent the Batman mythos for a new generation of fans, reimagining the Dark Knight as a working-class hero up against impossible odds (and the most terrifying foes ever), on a mission to prove that even in an era of wealth, power and corruption, one good person can change the world. When you take away the manor, the money, the advantages, what you’re left with is something absolute. No network yet.

Blue Beetle – Per Deadline’s first report over two years ago, Miguel Puga (The Casagrandes) was showrunner and director with Cristian Martinez (Women of the Movement, Good Trouble) set as writer of the animated series. Angel Manuel Soto and Gareth Dunnet-Alcocer, director and screenwriter of the 2023 film, respectively, were set to EP alongside John Rikard who served in the same capacity on the film.

Untitled Krypto Project – From EP C.H. Greenblatt. When he’s not hanging out with Superman or Supergirl, doggie Krypto tags along with a gang of misfit criminal wannabes who live down the block, and they soon discover he’s a ball of destructive, lovable energy worse than any of them. As he follows them into misadventures and poorly laid plans, Krypto’s pure nature slowly ends up redeeming them, whether they want it or not. No network yet.

Lanterns Season 2 – Chris Munday has assembled the writers room but no greenlight has been given to this HBO viewership hit. Lanterns’ Season 1 finale pulled in 10.5M global viewers in its first three days, a series high.

Poison Ivy – Tw-time Emmy-nominated The Penguin showrunner Lauren LeFranc is in talks to produce. In regards to a Penguin Season 2, there is nothing in the works as Batman II is the most immediate priority.

#3304. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3303. CleanupBuddy 2.0 expands beyond the keyboard with new display cleaning features

Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with CleanupBuddy, this is a nice little app that locks the keyboard to prevent accidental inputs while the user cleans it up.

Once they’re done cleaning, users can press and hold both Cmd keys to unlock the keyboard, then proceed to grease it up again.

The app also features a fun little animated character that reacts to your cleaning sessions with playful (and sometimes snarky) comments.

Today, CleanupBuddy was updated to version 2.0, with options to dim the display and ignore touch inputs, making it useful for users of both the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Macs with traditional displays.

You can use the new “Lock Touch Screen” option to block touch input while cleaning a supported touch screen. On Macs without a touch screen, the “Dim Display” option can still be used to darken the display for easier cleaning.

Today’s update also tweaks the in-app character, which now uses on-device Apple Intelligence to generate personalized comments before and after cleaning sessions, based on stats such as time spent cleaning, key presses, and mouse clicks.

Rambo explains that these stats are collected only during cleaning sessions and stored locally on the Mac, and that users can independently turn off both cleanup stats and Apple Intelligence integration in the app’s settings.

Other tweaks in today’s update include temporarily disabling Sticky Keys and its Shift-key shortcut during cleaning sessions, as well as improving the readability of the “Start Cleanup” button when using Liquid Glass.

CleanupBuddy 2.0 is available for $2.99 and is compatible with macOS 14 and later, while the new personalized messages require macOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled and its models ready to use.

#3302. La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX review

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are some of the best I’ve tested. They were instantly comfortable, durable on tough terrain, highly waterproof in storms, and offered exceptional traction across mud, gravel, and sand. However, despite good support and cushioning, they fit very narrow. Since La Sportiva offers no wide fit option, they won’t work for wider feet even if sized up.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I’ve been testing the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots for the last month on all of my hikes, and they’ve proved to be some of the best hiking boots for any season and any terrain. They look the part too, which helps me feel unstoppable on the trail.

The boots are comfortable out of the box and offer excellent traction as well as good cushioning and support on the trail. They are waterproof for all weather and are very durable with a tear-resistant upper.

Bear in mind that these boots have a narrow fit and don’t come in a wide size option, but that’s the only real downside to these excellent stompers. To find out more about my experience, you can keep reading this full La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX review.

Mocha/Redwood, Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood, Gravel/Cypress

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are available to purchase on the La Sportiva website for $249 in the U.S. and £220 in the U.K. The color selection differs between territories. In the U.S., there are only two choices — Carbon/Redwood or Mocha/Redwood — and in the U.K. you can choose from Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood or Gravel/Cypress. You can also purchase the shoes on Amazon for $310 in the U.S., but sizes and colors are limited.

When deciding on the boot size, you will need to convert from European sizing, since this is how the boots are sold on the site. The boots are available in women’s EUR sizes 36 to 42.5 with half sizes, and men’s EUR sizes 40 to 48.5 with half sizes. I’m usually a U.K. size 5 and needed to size up since the boots have a very snug fit. I ended up purchasing an EUR size 39, which is a U.K. size 6 and a U.S. women’s size 7.5.

These boots are certainly on the more expensive side, but it’s not hard to see why. They’re very well made and comfortable to walk in. Also very supportive are the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX. These boots cost $240, but this is the price to pay for a boot you’d happily spend your life walking in.

Another boot with excellent ankle support is the Keen Targhee IV, which costs $169. They’ve been my go-to boots for taking on the outdoors for over a year now, but I think the La Sportivas could end their reign.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

After speaking to friends and colleagues, it turns out the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots are a bit like cilantro — you either love it, or you hate it with a burning passion. But to me, they’re perfect. I like the look of the boots and the available colorways. They look like they mean business when you’re out on the trail.

The boots are perfect for narrow feet, and lace up for a snug, albeit supportive, fit. However, there’s no wide fit option, so those with wide feet need to look elsewhere, such as the Keen Targhee IV.

The upper is made from nubuck leather and a breathable Gore-Tex lining for a water-resistant finish. They coped well with heavy rain and deep puddles, and are also tear-resistant, so they can withstand even the rockiest terrain. The lacing system is very supportive, and cinched in all the right places to ensure a comfortable walk.

Although the laces get tight, my ankles moved freely. In other boots, I’ve been used to having a limited range of movement around my ankles like the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX, but these felt a lot more forgiving.

The La Sportiva boots have a footbed boost of 5mm, which is simply the insole height. This contributes to the cushioning of the boot and felt like it contoured to my feet. The drop value of 8mm (from heel to toe) also helped me get the best posture possible.

Usually, in other boots, I experience some strain on my lower back as a result of a smaller drop value, as there’s more pressure on my calves. Instead, I felt supported. The flex system with the CM EVE foam (a lightweight, rubber foam) also helps with rebound.

The outsole provided me with a lot of grip for every terrain I walked on. The lugs of the boot, which dig into the ground to provide traction, measure 4.5mm tall. This is a good height for grip and I find it to be the sweet spot, with most of my Keen boots also sitting in this range. The soles are made of Vibram rubber, so they absorb a lot of the impact of the ground, which helped reduce strain when walking over longer distances.

I have no complaints about the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots and their comfort level. I wore them right out of the box with no issues. My first walk in these boots took me through gravel, muddy fields, and shallow running water. The traction and flex felt great right off the bat.

The toe box of the boots is quite narrow, but this really wasn’t an issue for me. In fact, since my feet are very narrow, the ideal fit gave me more control, providing a more stable hiking experience.

My only very slight qualm is that my feet naturally swell from heat when walking, so the boots can start to feel a little tight. It’s obviously good that the lace-up system doesn’t slip, but sometimes, a little bit of give is a good thing, as you can move more freely. With that said, it didn’t cause me any major pain or blisters.

Cushioning in these boots is ideal. It took away some of the impact, especially when walking over bigger rocks and generally rough terrain, but I could still feel what was going on underfoot. The Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid boots also let you feel the ground beneath your feet through the soles, and this is a feature I’ve come to really appreciate.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easily some of my favorite boots.. They’re comfortable, cushioned, and support me across any terrain. The cushioning helps support my knees by reducing impact.

The 4.5mm lugs on the outsole of the hiking boots made me feel stable across all terrain I walked on. Even on slippery surfaces like wet rocks, the Vibram soles provided a lot of grip, and I didn’t slip once despite my clumsy disposition.

The arch support is great, and this in turn improved my posture. Since the lace-up system is tight for narrow feet, I felt a lot of support from the side walls — these two things combined stopped my feet from turning inward as I walked and boosted protection for my ankles by increasing my overall stability.

The boots have a moderate amount of flex, but never bent too much. I had complete support where I needed it. The most flex is happening in the toe box, which worked perfectly for me, especially when navigating uneven, tricky terrain.

Waterproofing on the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots is very effective. I went out hiking in the pouring rain, and my socks stayed completely dry. My walk also took me through puddles and shallow running water, and luckily my feet stayed dry and warm. I know I’ll be able to rely on these boots for all seasons.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easy to maintain, just like any other leather boot. If they get muddy on the trail, remove the laces and gently brush off any dry mud. Then, use a damp cloth to remove any stubborn stains. Let the boots air-dry naturally and avoid artificial heat, as it can compromise the boot's integrity.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are some of my favorite boots. They were comfortable and ready for a long walk right out of the box, and felt durable, even on trickier terrain. The boots provided excellent traction and stability across mud, gravel, and sand, and the waterproofing withstood stormy weather.

Although the cushioning and support are good, it’s worth noting that the boots fit narrowly. For people with wider feet, this boot simply won’t fit even if you size up, and unfortunately, La Sportiva doesn’t offer a wide fit option.

Nevertheless, this is still a great all-rounder boot to support you on the toughest adventures, and one I certainly recommend.
