#3301. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3300. iFixit tears down touchscreen MacBook Pro, reveals light-up Apple logo details

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

Finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

#3299. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3295. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

#3289. End of an era: Apple Support Community forums will permanently close on November 20

Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details.

If you have ever had a question or ran into a problem with an Apple product, chances are you have come across the Apple Support Community, the company’s official discussion forums where users from around the world help each other troubleshoot issues and share tips.

The platform has a history dating back to at least 1998, when it was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Since then, it was renamed Apple Discussions before relaunching as Apple Support Communities in April 2011, with a redesigned interface, personalized profiles, and a reputation system that rewarded users for helping others.

Tonight, however, users who tried to access the platform were greeted with the following message:

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Right now, the portal still shows a “Sign in” button, though it leads only to an AppleConnect login page labeled “AC Communities Web – Internal,” suggesting that access is now restricted to Apple employees.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

These forums were often far up when searching for Apple problems, but I’m not sure I ever found a real answer there. So often the threads went no where or someone would link an unhelpful Apple support page.

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with users able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled new submissions.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and clarification on the scope of the shutdown, and we’ll update this story if we hear back.

#3288. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3287. Reddit Reviews goes against the whole philosophy of the platform, say users

Many Redditors have expressed dismay at the launch of Reddit Reviews, a new AI-powered feature which aims to summarise posts about particular products.

Reddit is positioning the feature as a way to save time and effort when researching a potential purchase, but many Redditors say that replacing human interaction with AI summaries is antithetical to the whole philosophy of the platform – and is going to make the existing spam problem massively worse …

The value of customer reviews on ecommerce platforms like Amazon is becoming increasingly questionable thanks to practices like astroturfing by brands and offering people free products in return for five-star reviews.

That’s led to Reddit becoming one of the most trusted sources of feedback and advice on potential purchases, precisely because it’s a forum in which real people are free to express their true opinions. Indeed, many use a filter in their Google searches to draw content from Reddit specifically, adding the suffix ‘site:reddit.com’.

Reddit is increasingly a cesspool of maligned moderators (human and bot) and owners looking to make a bot. Posters on the platform are simply supplying free content with nothing to gain except bans when someone/somebot disagrees with them.

Reddit certainly isn’t immune to astroturfing – that is, fake posts by brands posing as ordinary users – but moderators put a lot of work into deleting spam and other inauthentic posts.

The platform yesterday announced the launch of Reddit Reviews, in which AI summarises the posts made about particular products and product categories. It’s being pitched as a way for people to save time when seeking the product opinions of Redditors.

Across Reddit’s communities, people discuss everything from hobbies and daily life to products they’re researching. By offering perspectives grounded in real experience, these conversations provide valuable context in every purchase decision journey […]

Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a new experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most important takeaways from across our communities.

However, as CNET spotted, the move has led to a backlash by many Redditors and subreddit moderators.

“I’ve already seen this in practice and it is a nightmare. It turns a basic conversation into an ad-ridden distracting mess. It’s horrible to read and had me fleeing every thread I saw it in.”

“I am a moderator on a couple of health subs and we explicitly do not allow advertisements because most of them are bullshit slop and completely predatory for vulnerable and newly diagnosed patients. We do not want, or need this, on our subs!”

“Yeah, this definitely isn’t going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site.”

“This is going to make our spam fighting even worse. This is horrible.”

“Every decision made by Reddit lately encourages spam and/or abuse that will make spam.”

“Not a single person who uses Reddit wants this.”

“You are incentivising existing spammers to continue or step up their activities, now that there’s a new well they can poison.”

I find it hard to disagree with the view that almost every monetization step the platform has made has degraded the user experience. This seems almost guaranteed to be another one.

#3286. The 10 Best Tech Deals From Walmart's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sale

The first of Walmart's three major sales for Black Friday and Cyber Monday is now live, and there are already some amazing tech deals to take advantage of. I've gathered my top ten tech products from the sale to make your life a little easier. For more, keep tabs on our Black Friday coverage, where we post the latest deals from not just Walmart, but Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers' Black Friday deals.

Apple's latest smartwatch is the Series 12, but don't count out the Series 11. By sacrificing a few of Apple's newest features, you can save some money on the more premium version of this last-gen Apple Watch. Right now, the Titanium Series 11 GPS + cellular model is on sale for $699. That's $100 according to Walmart, but really, you're saving $50—this version of the Series 11 was $799 when it launched, but now, the Titanium Series 12 is $749.

During WWDC 26 earlier this summer, Apple announced new Siri AI upgrades with watchOS 27—but only some Apple Watches have compatibility. Luckily, the Series 11 is one of them, at least for many of them. Some other upgrades in the new OS include a dedicated Siri app, a new app grid, a new single-tap gesture, among other features. Just note that only Series 12 and Ultra 4 can run Audio Intelligence.

Bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. They use a technology that sends audio vibrations to your inner ear while leaving your ear canals open. Shokz is one of, if not the best, brands making bone conduction headphones right now. At the high end of Shokz's offerings sit the OpenRun Pro 2, which impressed me when I tested them out for review. Amazon currently has a restored pair for $95 (originally $135.95 and $179.99 new).

Beats are a more affordable Apple alternative to AirPods, and you can often find them with substantial discounts. You can now get the Beats Solo 4 for $69 (originally $199.95) after a 50% discount. These on-ear headphones are Siri-compatible, so you don't need to use your iPhone to ask the assistant questions. They also have personalized spatial audio, which produces "3D audio" that follows the movement of your iPhone (as long as that media supports spatial audio), as well as an impressive battery life of 50 hours.

Most, if not all, TV speakers aren't great. While you have plenty of options, the quickest and least expensive way to improve your TV's audio capabilities to buy a soundbar. Compare a soundbar's size to the thin, small speakers jammed into modern TVs. The Vizio 4.1 Pro Soundbar and rear speakers come with Dolby Atmos support and cost just $79 (originally $148). They won't win any audio awards, but it's better than any built-in TV speakers, and for $79, it'll improve your experience without breaking the bank.

If you want to take things up a notch, consider this 5.1 channel sound system. Not only does it include far more channels than a single soundbar, but you're also adding a dedicated subwoofer to the mix. A subwoofer will make those thuds, explosions, and low vibrations much more pronounced than on a soundbar alone. For $149.99 (originally $249.99), you can get the ULTIMEA 5.1 surround sound system, which comes with a soundbar—replicating left, right, and center channels—two rear speakers, and a subwoofer.

I love projectors and Roku. To me, a Roku projector just makes sense, especially at $99.97 (originally $389.99). This projector is portable and has the Roku OS already installed, so it's easy to project it against a wall, ceiling, or screen, whether it's indoors or outdoors. It's easy to set up; you just need an outlet nearby and to dim or turn off the lights. If you have Bluetooth speakers, you can hook them up to create a more immersive sound.

The TCL Q51GB is a QLED Google TV that is a great value for anyone looking for size, color, and features. The 98-inch class is heavily discounted at its $898 price (originally $1,499.99). TCL makes one of the best QLEDs for the money, and their technology keeps getting better. This TV supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, and if you're a gamer, you get a refresh rate of 240Hz that is automatically triggered with its Auto Game Mode feature.

Gaming monitors can get pricey fast. At $179.99 (originally $299.99), this 27-inch Samsung Odyssey G55C curved gaming monitor offers a 1440p resolution, a 1000R curve, a 165Hz refresh rate with FreeSync and G-SYNC compatibility to keep screen tearing to a minimum, and features like Samsung’s Virtual Aim Point and Contrast Enhancer. It's a solid choice for gaming, especially at this price point.

Alienware makes great gaming laptops, and the Aurora is a great option for anyone who wants to get all the essentials without spending too much. At its current $1,099 price (originally $1,999), the Alienware Aurora 16 becomes a mid-tier gaming laptop at a "budget" price. We reviewed the higher-tier Aurora 16X and were impressed with it. The Aurora 16 has a slightly slower processor, a dimmer display with half the refresh rate, a smaller battery, and a weaker graphics card, but given its price, it's great for a gamer looking for a solid gaming laptop in the $1,000 range.

Walmart has the AirPods 4 without ANC for $89 (originally $129.99). This model comes with USB-C charging (no more Lightning charging). These are powered by Apple's H2 chip, so you'll get Personalized Spatial Audio and the ability to use head gestures to tell Siri "yes" or "no" (this also works for answering or denying calls). They are rated IP54 for dust and water resistance, offer up to five hours of listening per charge (up to 30 hours with the charging case), and can handle automatic switching with your other Apple devices. You can read more about the non-ANC AirPods in PCMag's "excellent" review.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

#3285. Poetry for Engineers: Of Code and Shortleaf Pine

Read Ralph Earle’s poem from the November 2026 issue

After retiring from IBM as a senior software engineer in 2017, Ralph Earle has published two poetry collections.

I step into the warm moist airamong the columns of the pines,their net of twigs and rootscomplex as any lines of code.

The trees purify and anchor.Their branches balance my restlessness.

Their calling is to be present,mine to develop apps. Our tasksverge toward a common logic:living filaments of root, of interface.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. While at IBM, he coauthored Enterprise Computing with Objects: From Client/Server Environments to the Internet for Addison-Wesley’s Bloch-Jacobson-Rumbaugh Object Technology Series, and he published articles in technical journals, including IEEE Computer Magazine, IBM Systems Journal, Distributed Computing, Management Directions, and Object Magazine.

In retirement, Earle has flourished in a second career as a poet. His poetry collections are Everything You Love Is New (Redhawk Publications, 2024) and The Way the Rain Works (Sable Books, 2015). He has been nominated for the Pushcart Prize three times and comanages a monthly poetry series at a Chapel Hill, N.C., bookstore. His poems have appeared in many print and online outlets, including The Sun, Carolina Quarterly, and Sufi Journal.

The third quarter is typically our slowest period of the year due to summer vacation schedules, and the first quarter tends to benefit from license renewal activity. For the first nine months of 2026, total revenue rose 14%, and our net loss has improved by 42%, a solid step in the right direction. I want to spend a moment on why we're seeing growing new business wins and how they relate to our core biometric expertise built over decades, which is gaining recognition as a real differentiator where identity assurance matters most.

Areas such as government, defense, and financial services, the regulated industries, these customers know how, with uncertainty, that a person, the actual individual accessing a critical system, is who they claim to be. That's what our Identity-Bound Biometrics deliver, tying access to the individual rather than to a device, a phone, a token, or a password that can be shared, stolen, or phished. Regulators are increasingly pushing in this direction. In response to growing incidents of systems compromise, in the UAE, for example, the central bank directed banks and other licensed financial institutions to phase out SMS and email one-time passwords earlier this year in favor of stronger methods, including biometrics and passkeys.

Policies like these are important tailwinds for the value our solutions provide. That backdrop is showing up in who's choosing BIO-key and in the size of the opportunities. Our international team is increasingly winning larger, high-profile deals in highly regulated sectors, as I mentioned before, such as government and banking. In Portugal, a national security agency selected BIO-key and our partner, Visualforma, to secure access to its administrative systems, privileged accounts, and critical applications. We are seeing incredible upside in the international markets, in particular in the Middle East and in Europe. These awards bring us to eight new Middle East region customers in roughly seven months. These are among the most security-conscious organizations anywhere, and each deployment becomes an important proof of concept and reference for the next, and that's what we're seeing now. This traction is built on strong local distribution and integration partners with strong connections and understanding of each customer's needs.

We continue to expand our partner network, such as our recent partnership with Al Majlis Group to extend our reach across the Arabian Gulf. We have also begun establishing a BIO-key subsidiary in Saudi Arabia to support our growing government business there that will also be staffed with BIO-key resources. Overall, the opportunity is very large, and Gartner forecasts end-user information security spending in the Middle East and North Africa will reach approximately $4 billion in 2026. It's starting to be reflected in our results as the third quarter revenue from our Europe, Middle East, and South America region grew 39% with license fees more than doubling.

In Europe, we recently launched a technology integration with Cipher, the cybersecurity division of global security group Prosegur, bringing our IAM, biometric, and password technologies into their portfolio, starting in Portugal with plans to explore other markets where they operate, such as in Spain, the U.S., and in Brazil. In the U.S., our focus is on PortalGuard, our flexible IAM platform supporting 16 factors of authentication, including fingerprint, face, and palm biometrics. We continue to roll out our latest version, PortalGuard 7, across our customer base. In October, we recruited cybersecurity veteran Steve Morrow as President of PortalGuard to accelerate adoption.

In the realm of AI, our new internally developed Passkey:YOU authenticator received full FIDO Alliance certification this September. It is now in final testing ahead of its major launch, which will allow us to leapfrog the capabilities of our earlier outsourced solution. Our Passkey:YOU solution lets employees sign in with a fingerprint scanner or badge rather than a phone or a token, and it positions us for one of the most important emerging identity challenge, AI agents. This year, the FIDO Alliance formed a working group to develop standards for trusted AI agent interactions.

We believe that for the highest risk actions, the answer has to be verified human, not password or device acknowledgment. Our Identity-Bound Biometrics can tie approval of sensitive AI-driven actions to the actual person accountable. This agentic AI authentication and authorization is an important aspect of the integrated offering of our new Cipher relationship. Steve Morrow, as I mentioned, the President of our PortalGuard group, is leading the development of the product plans in this area. We see this as a meaningful new market opportunity alongside our core workforce and customer authentication business. On the financial side, we strengthened our balance sheet considerably in the third quarter.

We retired our remaining note and debt, leaving us effectively debt-free, and we currently have a solid cash and working capital position to fund our business. Looking ahead, our recent wins, growing base of recurring license revenue, and a solid pipeline of regulated industry opportunities across EMEA position us for a solid finish to 2026 and a really strong start to 2027, supported by the annual license renewal of our largest customer, which exceeds $1 million. We expect roughly $1.2 million in annual license fee renewals in the first quarter alone, and we are targeting profitability as we approach that timeframe.

Our deep biometric expertise, marquee government and financial customers, growing high-margin software revenue, streamlined cost structure, and cleaner balance sheet gives us a very strong foundation, and we believe it sets the stage for an exciting future period. I will hand the call over to Ceci to take you through the financials in more detail. Ceci?

Ceci Welch: Thanks, Mike, and good morning, everyone. We issued our third quarter results this morning via the press release, and we expect to file our Form 10-Q either later today or on Monday. I will review some of the key items. Total revenue for our Q3 2026 was $1.48 million compared to $1.55 million in Q3 2025. License fee revenue increased 39% to $1.28 million, reflecting several new customer license deployments and representing 86% of total revenue versus 59% a year ago. Hardware revenue was $12,000 compared to $364,000 in Q3 2025, as our Q3 2025 included a large hardware deployment for a long-term customer.

Sales, maintenance, and other revenue decreased 27% to $195,000 due to the timing of our agreement renewals as well as the impact of our partner-led sales model. Virtually all of our integrated business is sold through channel partners who typically provide implementation and sales support themselves. For the first nine months, revenue increased 14% to $5.55 million, again driven by the 37% increase in license fee revenue. Gross profit increased 12% to $1.34 million, and gross margin improved 90% from 77% in Q3 2025, reflecting a greater portion of license fee revenue as a percentage of total revenue. Gross margin has improved sequentially in each quarter this year from 83% in Q1 to 87% in Q2 and 90% in Q3.

For the first nine months, it improved 86% from 77%. Operating expenses increased 4% year-over-year, but decreased 2% sequentially from Q2. SG&A increased 9%, reflecting higher administrative and personnel costs and annual meeting costs, while research, development, and engineering expenses decreased 7% for the first nine months. Operating expense decreased 1% to $6.29 million. Our Q3 2026 operating loss improved to $820,000 from $892,000. Our net loss improved $886,000 from $965,000 in Q3 2025. Including a non-cash deemed dividend of $4.5 million related to the August warrant inducement, net loss available to common stockholders was $5.9 million, or $4 per share, compared to $965,000, or $1.44 per share in Q3 2025.

The deemed dividend is an accounting entry with no impact on our operating loss, cash, or stockholders' equity. For the first nine months, our net loss improved 42% to $1.67 million from $2.87 million. Including the deemed dividend, net loss available to common stockholders was $6.17 million, or $5.37 per share, compared to $2.87 million, or $4.87 per share. Per-share results reflect the April 30th 1-for-10 reverse split, as well as the warrant exercises and other financing activities. Turning to the balance sheet, stockholders' equity increased to $6.5 million at September 30th from $4.3 million at June 30th.

We ended the quarter with $5.3 million in current assets, including $2.2 million of cash and $2.4 million of accounts receivable, and $367,000 of net inventory. Working capital improved to $3.1 million at the close of the third quarter 2026 from $0.8 million in June 30th, 2026. During the quarter, we retired the remaining balance of our note payable, leaving us free of our note debt, and only remaining is a small euro-based loan of approximately EUR 12,000 that will be paid off by the end of the year. In August, we raised gross proceeds of $2.5 million through the warrant inducement transaction. As Mike outlined, we expect a solid finish in 2026 and a strong start to 2027.

That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone keypad. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If at any time a question has been addressed and you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then two. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. The first question comes from Jack Vander Aarde with Maxim Group. Please go ahead.

Jack Vander Aarde: Okay, great. Good morning. I appreciate the update, and thanks for taking my questions.

Jack Vander Aarde: Mike, good morning, Mike. I will start with a question on the third quarter revenues. Good to see the strong license growth, and that has been consistent. I am wondering for the hardware line, sometimes you have some orders and timing of delays that get some slippage. Were we expecting a big hardware order in 3Q, or did anything get pushed into 4Q?

Mike DePasquale: Yeah. I think starting in Q2, we had a larger hardware order that we were expecting for an international customer that we have been working for quite some time. That has just been pushed, and that is the nature of these large kind of civil ID government programs. They sometimes get deployed on time, sometimes they get extended. That larger hardware order has been pushed. Again, given that happened, obviously our revenue would have been much, much higher. That is also hardware product that, as you know, we fully own and has been in our inventory for a considerable period of time. So, it is also all margin and cash and profit for us.

We are selling the hardware, but it is just happening in smaller tranches, and so it is dribbling. We expect we will continue to sell that hardware through the end of this year and certainly into the beginning of next year.

Jack Vander Aarde: Okay. I appreciate the color there. It sounds like it's not a lost opportunity, just smaller batches, and will be recognized over time. The gross margin is very strong here. It's actually, I think on a blended overall basis, one of the strongest quarters in your history. That's good to see.

Mike DePasquale: It is. It is. For sure, what we're seeing is, again, as I mentioned in my prepared remarks, we're seeing very, very strong license revenue. There's hardware as well in this. Sometimes it happens before, sometimes it happens after the sale in our EMEA group in the regulated space.

Jack Vander Aarde: As a follow-up to that, Mike, you're clearly having some great success in the Middle East. It's really ramping up. I think you mentioned eight new material customers out there. I imagine this plays a role in shaping 2027. Do you feel like you're going to be entering 2027 and even 4Q 2026 on the licensing front? How do these new customer wins, I guess, if you could quantify or just directionally, how does this set you up for, I guess, entering 2027?

Mike DePasquale: Well, it kind of sets us up, number one, to be profitable, number two, to be consistently profitable, and number three, to potentially be cash flow positive and remain cash flow positive. When you're doing high-end six-figure and seven-figure deals, the cash flow is wonderful. When it's all software, the margins are incredible. Even again, we're going to see some larger hardware orders come along with this, because typically, these larger entities, when they deploy our technology, they're deploying biometrics, and so they need not only to enroll all of their employees or customers, but they need to have the facility to be able to identify them, and so our finger scanners get pulled along.

I mean, I just think we're in an incredible position. We've never been in this position before, where we're sitting on enough cash and receivables to really fund our business for a couple of years, and with a pipeline of seven-figure opportunities that we obviously will be working in the next six months. It's just an entirely different opportunity for us today. And it's because of the dynamics that we're seeing in the world, right? We've always had a very strong business, as you know, in the defense sector, international defense sector. We have a very large customer that's deployed over 60,000 of our devices and enrolled hundreds of thousands of their folks.

This is now traveling to all of the other, right, sensitive government and financial services institutions on an international basis. I don't want to discount also our domestic business. That casino win, which again, was a Q4, that's a Q4 opportunity that was not recognized in Q3, so it'll be recognized this quarter, is really kind of a resurgence and a reinvigoration of our domestic business with partners. We are really going full bore, similar in nature to the way we operate in EMEA, partner, partner-centric. I think that's going to have a huge impact on our domestic business as well.

Jack Vander Aarde: Great. I'm glad you mentioned the casino win again. I wanted to just kind of follow up with that and just your thoughts on, I guess, the overall casino gaming hospitality space for BIO-key, bigger picture. Then also just touching on, obviously, the agentic AI update that you mentioned. How does this agentic AI space and opportunity and this new casino space, just how does this compare relative to, I guess, the upside you're seeing in EMEA, in defense, your other core verticals that are large?

Mike DePasquale: Yeah. Just a couple of questions there. Let's go and answer the gaming one first. It's interesting because in gaming, they're struggling with a very typical security issue or problem that most enterprises are, where you can't use a phone or a token, you have a very serious security issue and problem because you need multi-factor authentication in order to meet your compliance hurdles. Being able to just place your finger and automatically authenticate and not have to have a phone or a token or a card, right, which can be shared and used by anyone, we have the perfect solution. This was our first entry. We did this deal from start to finish.

This was a WEB-key, not WEB-key, it was a web lead that came into us, right? It was an inbound lead from inception to close was less than 60 days, because they have a serious issue. Also, this customer, and this is a six-figure deal, multiple number six-figure deal, a three-year contract. But this customer is also taking us to an event in the first quarter where we will have the opportunity to share what we are doing for them with other potential prospects. Gaming is a big business in this country, not just the big names like MGM and the ones that you know in Vegas.

There are an incredible number of tribal, local casinos and resorts in almost every state in the country. It is a really, really nice opportunity for us. That is the gaming question. How does that relate against the EMEA scenario? Clearly, the deals in defense and banking are, some of them are seven-figure, many of them are seven-figure deals, so they are bigger deals, right? Those are much bigger deals than even enterprise opportunities. Again, there is a balance. Do I think on the domestic side we can get to that point? I do. I think it is going to take us some time, but I think we can. As it relates to agentic AI, look, it is intuitive.

You are hearing it all over. Agents are wonderful. They are incredible in terms of the efficiency and productivity that they can provide to enterprise and government agencies. The problem is, if they operate on their own without any human intervention, there is always a danger and a risk that they go rogue or you cannot meet your compliance requirements and/or you put your customers at risk. In the real world of agentic AI, you want a human to acknowledge and to validate and authenticate that agent to do very specific tasks on behalf of you or the company.

Validating that with a biometric, ensuring that the individual who authorizes that, who says, "Yes, this agent can go out and do X, Y, Z," knowing who they are and when they validated and authenticated that process is critical and important. We see that as a really, really big opportunity because AI is dominating the space in enterprise and government, and securing AI agents is a real issue, and human intervention is not an option, it is required. I suspect with the new legislative changes past election here last week, we are going to see a lot more pressure to reel that in and ensure that we are securing and locking down agents so they do not go rogue.

Jack Vander Aarde: Got it. I appreciate all the color there. I know that was a loaded question. But no, that's encouraging to hear, Mike. My last question, then I'll hop in the queue, is just on the outlook and kind of relative to last quarter's outlook. I think you were targeting profitability in the back half of this year. Now, that's probably not quite on track now, but third quarter was close to break-even operating income. Wondering if you could just share more of an update on your, I guess, more of a precise update on your outlook for 2027.

Jack Vander Aarde: Has anything changed? Are you expecting growth and profitability? Just any other color would be helpful. Thanks, Mike.

Mike DePasquale: Yeah. I'm really expecting significant growth, and I still think even in the fourth quarter here, we're going to see very strong finish. I'd like, obviously, we're targeting profitability and we're targeting to be cash flow positive. But certainly, as we go into the strongest quarter for our company, the first quarter, with the kind of pipeline we have and the opportunities that we're working right now, I'm highly encouraged we're going to see significant growth. We're certainly going to be profitable growth. Again, we're not in the market from a cash perspective to have to raise capital or to do anything from a financial perspective to support the company.

We have enough resource right now to be able to do that.

Jack Vander Aarde: Okay, great. I appreciate the color, Mike. Thank you.

Operator: Again, if you have a question, please press star then one. The next question comes from Dan Kamhis, private investor. Please go ahead.

Dan Kamhis: Morning. Along with the gross margins, your account receivables have been on a significant upward trend, now up to $2.35 million from $0.96 million a year ago. That is about 245%, while your payables and accrued expenses have been fine in the same period. It is also interesting that in the weak third quarter, the AR was up significantly. I am wondering if that increase is fairly distributed, or did it come from one or two customers, such as that bank renewal you mentioned?

Mike DePasquale: Well, it did not come from a bank renewal, it came from new customers. I think in my prepared remarks, I mentioned that we were kind of on a tear, right, in terms of closing new business, especially in the Middle East. A couple of those deals are pretty large. It is a balance, but it is definitely a reflection of the opportunities that we the new business opportunities that we closed in Q3.

Dan Kamhis: Okay. With that kind of collectible, I mean, couldn't that result in a break-even cash flow by itself in the fourth quarter?

Mike DePasquale: Yeah, we hope it will. It is timing of collections, right? Keep in mind, all this business comes through partners, and so, we are always cautious about collections and staying on top of things. But yeah, it certainly can.

Dan Kamhis: What about this trend in AR? Do you consider that I mean, it sounds like you consider it's either going to continue, or do you think it's peaked? Will it stay at this level? Just color on what you see in AR.

Mike DePasquale: I think it can continue if we close larger deals, right? I mean, it depends on how much business we close. I think we're very encouraged by what we have in front of us for Q4 and Q1, and we have insight into Q2. So, that trend should continue. Look, I would be happy if it dipped a little bit and we collected more, and so the receivables were down, but our cash collections were up. That's a dynamic that we'll see how that unfolds.

Dan Kamhis: Solid fourth quarter. I looked at some of your past results on the fourth quarter. They've been, I don't know, they average about one I think last year was $1.24 million. By solid, do you mean comparable to the results of the last quarters, or these last fourth quarters, or? It sounds like you think solid might be even.

Mike DePasquale: Well, okay, first of all, I don't have in my head last year's fourth quarter revenue number. Ceci, I don't know if you have that available, because I don't have a mark to measure against.

Ceci Welch: Yeah, let me look real quick.

Mike DePasquale: Okay. Dan, once Ceci comes back with the number, I will be able to articulate, do I think it is going to be significantly over that or whatever. I do not want to fly, just throw numbers out. But, yeah, we are.

Ceci Welch: Yeah. Last year was $1.188 million. The year before that was $1.286 million. The year before that was $1.593 million.

Mike DePasquale: Got it. And that was fourth quarter, correct? Fourth quarter numbers.

Ceci Welch: Correct. These are fourth quarter numbers. Yeah.

Mike DePasquale: Yeah. We'll have significant growth over that in this fourth quarter. Yes. And it will be significant.

Dan Kamhis: That's great. The agentic AI authentication market, could that be a killer app for you that actually opens up the U.S. market?

Mike DePasquale: Absolutely. In fact, it's funny, internally we're calling it a killer app. I don't like to use it in our. But we're calling it a killer app because we do believe it's something that, first of all, including our passkey, it can attach anywhere. It doesn't matter what IDP, in other words, what maybe security infrastructure you're using. For example, even if you're using Okta or you're using Ping or SailPoint, whatever you're using, you can attach our biometric agentic solution, right, on top of that, without having to load tremendous amounts of software and infrastructure. We do see that as a killer app, and we'll be deploying that to customers this quarter.

Into 2027, we think this is going to be a really, really big partner-centric, right, solution, where these partners have existing customers. They can take this as an upsell and an add-on, which they love, right, because they always want to add services and support and technologies for their existing base. That is how they make money. Dan Kamhis: You are talking about the U.S. market, right?

They continue to bring you to their customer base. We got to close the first handful, and we got to hold their hand through it, and we do that.

The products that we're developing, we're developing for partners to be able to go out, manage, demo, manage, and sell on their own without our intervention. That's what these partners want. They want something that's really simple, straightforward. They can demo it. They have a dashboard to be able to market the licenses and sell it, and then sell any hardware if that's required beyond that.

Dan Kamhis: Got it. Should we expect increasing R&D expenditures in this area then over the next 12 months?

Dan Kamhis: Great. Mentioned a multiple six-figure deal on the casino. Was that for a single resort or is it a whole chain?

Dan Kamhis: On some of these other deals in the Middle East and Portugal, so that I have a feel for the actual size or potential.

I am not sure that the public really understands the opportunity with Prosegur. I do not know if you know anything about Prosegur, but they are a very, very large physical security company. Dan Kamhis: Wow. That is great. Just to clarify on the hardware sale, you said it is pushed. Does that mean it is basically on hold or not happening the next couple quarters?

Dan Kamhis: You mean to this customer that was going to buy the big amount or?

Mike DePasquale: Correct. They are our partners, so they have multiple contracts, right? So it is not one end user customer, it is multiple customers of theirs.

Dan Kamhis: Okay. Got a couple questions on the balance sheet, if that's okay. The Boumarang asset was, I think, written down in the 10-K. What's the probability there's going to be additional write-downs on that?

Mike DePasquale: Nothing that we're aware of.

Ceci Welch: Yeah. We have been following their public filings, and now they have one of the big reasons for the write-down last year was because they were not getting revenue yet, and they now have a contract where they're getting revenue. Some improvement there along with the next one. So, yeah. It's in their published filing.

Dan Kamhis: Okay. Great. That's good news then. Maybe you'll have to write it up. On the warrants, I noticed the shareholders approved the $4 warrants. I guess you're kind of indicating there's no real chance that you'll need to sell additional shares and create even additional warrants to reduce the price of those warrants at this point? Clarify that, I guess, one more time.

Mike DePasquale: No reason at all. On the other hand, if it hangs in the $5, $6, $7 range, maybe they won't. But we have no intention of doing anything in the context of another inducement, or we don't really need the cash, and we don't have the need to do that right now. I don't see that. But if they do exercise, it brings cash into the company. They're priced at $4.02 or $4.10, Ceci? I forget which.

Mike DePasquale: Yeah. $4.06. We'll see what happens.

Dan Kamhis: Yeah. Speaking of stock price, I noticed the short interest was at 10,000 shares during the summer, and it shot up to 1 million shares on the 30th, about half the share count. Actually, it is down to maybe 270,000. I am wondering if this increase in the short interest, whether you consider it has anything to do with these days where we trade 10, 40, 80 times the float?

Mike DePasquale: Yeah, it is hard to say, Dan. We do not really understand that dynamic. Look, I have been dealing with this now for two years, and I talk to a lot of people, advisors, so forth and so on, and it is hard to say, right? We know it is bots, we know it is machine trading, it is algorithmic trading. Unfortunately, in fact, our IR guys were saying this morning, the volatility is creating big upside for traders, right? They love volatility because you make it on the upside and you make it on the downside.

So, when we have an announcement and the stock runs and we trade 100 million shares or 200 million shares, it is just people, not people, it is institutions, entities, whatever, making money in and out, right? 200 and something thousand shares short is about 10% of the outstanding, right? We have 2,035,000 shares outstanding, so if there is 200-something thousand shares shorted, it is 10%, not out of the realm of reality. You can borrow the shares in certain Schwab, and Fidelity will loan shares, but there just are not that many to loan. So, I think we have to deal with that. But 200,000 shares on 2,035,000 outstanding is not what I would consider material.

Dan Kamhis: Yeah. No, not when you are trading 100 million shares. Okay, last question. If we take the cash and the AR minus the payables and accrued liabilities, that is about $3 million. Price of $2.20 right now, times one. Well, your float or your stated share count, I think, in your current document is 1.35 million. That is about $3 million also. So, it seems to me your company is currently trading essentially for cash. Considering your buying window opens in a couple days for a month, should we expect to see insider buying in the near future?

Dan Kamhis: Okay. That is the answer I like to hear. Okay, I appreciate all the time, and hopefully the coming quarters will be good. Thank you.
