#3193. Google’s Gemini can now read your Google Wallet to help you budget

Users can link bank and card accounts too, but Google may train AI on summaries of their transactions.

Google Wallet joins Gmail, Photos, YouTube and Search as an app Gemini can connect to through Personal Intelligence.

Google is rolling out a Google Wallet connection to all Gemini app users in the US. Gemini can analyse spending, find subscriptions and suggest budgets, with read-only access. Google says it may train AI on summaries of that data if users keep activity on.

Google is letting every Gemini app user in the US connect Google Wallet, so the chatbot can answer questions about their spending, the company announced on Thursday. Users can also link bank and credit card accounts through Plaid for more detailed answers.

After tagging @Google Wallet in a chat, users can ask Gemini to chart last quarter’s spending or help them save $1,000. It can also find subscriptions that went up in price, or use last year’s spending to suggest a holiday budget.

The connection is opt-in and read-only. Gemini can see account data but cannot move, manage or invest money, and users can switch it off at any time. That differs from Google’s Universal Cart, which already lets Gemini take payments.

Google says it does not train its AI directly on Wallet data. But its help pages say that if users keep their Gemini activity on, it may train on summaries of their transactions. Some of those chats may also be read by human reviewers.

Google also launched Memory Summary, a page showing what Gemini remembers about a user, such as their goals and preferences. Users can edit or delete those details. It is not available in Europe or the UK.

#3192. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

Apple continues to expand the appeal of its free Sports app, which focuses on delivering real-time sports scores and stats, across many different sports.

#3188. Cornelis launches CN6000 800G networking to rival Nvidia InfiniBand

Its new 800G network cards aim to stop costly AI chips from sitting idle while they wait for data.

Cornelis’s CN6000 network card and switch, which partner systems will use from early 2027.

Cornelis, which Intel spun out in 2020, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI and supercomputers. It claims lower latency than Nvidia’s InfiniBand, based on its own tests. Partner systems arrive in early 2027.

Cornelis, a networking company spun out of Intel, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI clusters and supercomputers, it announced this week. It is pitching them as a rival to Nvidia’s InfiniBand.

In large AI systems, thousands of chips must constantly swap data. If the network is slow, expensive chips sit idle. “Every minute an accelerator waits on the network is capacity our customers paid for and didn’t use,” said CEO Lisa Spelman.

The main card uses Omni-Path, a networking technology Intel dropped in 2019 before spinning the business off as Cornelis in 2020. Cornelis says the card can handle 1.6 billion messages a second. It also says it is 21% faster than Nvidia’s InfiniBand at passing a small message, though that comes from its own tests.

A faster single message does not mean jobs finish 21% sooner, since that depends on the workload. Cornelis also launched a card for standard Ethernet networks, which most AI data centres use, with support for the newer Ultra Ethernet standard due later.

The cards work with chips from AMD, Intel, Nvidia and Qualcomm. Dell, Lenovo and Supermicro are among the server makers planning to support them, with systems due in early 2027.

Networking has become a hot spot in AI. Nvidia has spent billions on optical links, Huawei is betting on wiring over chips, and startups such as Upscale AI are building ways to connect rival chips. AMD, a Cornelis partner, is also building rack-scale systems to compete with Nvidia.

#3187. Digi Power X (DGXX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

AI now drives nearly half of revenue as the Columbiana facility nears launch.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Digi Power X Inc. (DGXX +3.17%) reported a transition toward AI infrastructure operations, as AI-related services now represent nearly half of the total revenue mix. Management stated that the company is focusing on completing its Columbiana facility and scaling the NeoCloudz platform to capture increasing demand for inference processing. The company confirmed that Phase I tenant access is scheduled for December 15, 2026, while the forward capital plan prioritizes growth through customer prepayments and project-level debt to minimize equity dilution. Management reported that the scarcity of permitted power assets is increasing the value of its current infrastructure portfolio.

Moderator: Good morning, and welcome to the Digi Power X Inc.'s Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. Please note that this event is being recorded, and a transcript will be available on Digi Power X Inc.'s website. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A brief question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. Unless noted otherwise, all amounts referred to during this call are denominated in U.S. dollars. Certain comments made during this call may include forward-looking statements or forward-looking information within the meaning of applicable U.S. and Canadian securities laws, including statements regarding the company's 2027 outlook, capital plan, and anticipated financing.

Such statements and information reflect current expectations and are, as such, are subject to a variety of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from current expectations. Those risks and uncertainties include, but are not limited to, factors discussed in Digi Power X Inc.'s report on Form 10-Q for the three and nine months ended September 30th, 2026, and the annual report for the year ended December 31st, 2025, as well as the company's other disclosure documents. Except to the extent required by applicable law, Digi Power X undertakes no obligation to publicly update or review any forward-looking statements.

During the call, management may make reference to certain Non-GAAP financial measures that are not separately defined under GAAP, such as EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA. Management believes that those Non-GAAP measures, when considered in conjunction with GAAP financial measures, provide useful information for both management and investors. Reconciliations between GAAP and Non-GAAP measures are presented in tables accompanying the press release highlighting Digi Power X financial results for the quarter ended September 30th, 2026, which has been filed and made accessible under the company's continuous disclosure profile on SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca, and is also available on the SEC's EDGAR website at www.sec.gov/edgar. I'd now like to turn the call over to Michel Amar, CEO of Digi Power X.

Michel Amar: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today as we share our results for the third quarter of 2026 for Digi Power X. Our third quarter results show that Digi Power X transformation into AI infrastructure company is beginning to take hold. Third quarter 2026 highlights. Our revenue went up 85% to $12.25 million from the second quarter of 2026, and up 50% from the third quarter of 2025. AI revenue of $5.66 million, up more than 400% from the second quarter, and representing now 46% of total revenue, compared with no AI revenue in the third quarter of 2025.

GPU rental bare metal through NeoCloudz of $2.46 million, up 127% from the second quarter, compared with no GPU rental revenue in the third quarter of 2025. Energy sales through our power plant of $3.29 million, up 68% from the second quarter, and 9% year-over-year. Legacy Bitcoin activities fell to approximately 27% of revenue from 63% a year ago. AI revenue more than offset that decline. EBITDA of positive EBITDA of $6.5 million and positive adjusted EBITDA of $600,000 compared with $1.7 million and $-1 million respectively in the third quarter of 2025. Positive net income of $1 million, materially supported by digital currency and warrant valuation gains, compared with net income of $100,000 in the third quarter of 2025.

Let's talk about the balance sheet and liquidity as of September 30, 2026. Cash and cash equivalents and digital currencies of $119.6 million. Working capital of $103 million, compared with $17.5 million at September 30, 2025. Digital currency holding of $24.5 million, up 66% year-over-year. Net fixed assets of $145.6 million, up 646% year-over-year, reflecting infrastructure investment primarily at the Columbiana, Alabama facility. No outstanding borrowing as of today. Balance sheet and liquidity as of today, November 13. The company's cash equivalents is approximately a little bit above $100 million cash. $168 million year-to-date capital expenditure deployed towards GPU equipment and data center build-out at the Columbiana, Alabama facility. Operational highlights and outlook. Columbiana, Alabama AI campus.

Construction of phase I remain on schedule. We expect to give our tenant access to the phase I facility on December 15, 2026. Basically, in 4.5 weeks from now. We'll start conditioning all the liquid cooling and power system at that time. With phase I billing expected to begin in January 2027. Work on phase II has started already for a few months, and subject to various conditions, we are targeting tenant access for phase II in March 2027. We are on schedule to be also on time to give access. A lot of the investment has been towards phase II already.

Our 10-year take-or-pay colocation agreement with our tenant, Cerebras, our AI colocation tenant at Columbiana is expected to provide phase I fees averaging approximately $40 million per year over the 10-year term, or approximately $402 million in total. Phase II would add approximately $58.5 million in annual fees, bringing combined average annual fees to approximately $107 million per year, and a total contract value to approximately $1.07 billion for both phases. The agreement also includes an option to extend the relationship for an additional term, which could increase the total potential contract value to approximately $2.5 billion. NeoCloudz Token Factory is live.

We launched this quarter from Berlin, our Token Factory, taking Digi Power X from AI infrastructure provider to direct seller of AI tokens. Running on our own power, data centers, and GPUs, the platform sells AI inference straight to customers. The huge advantage of that are the margins. We see margins anywhere from 85% to 90%, actual margins. So it's a business that will create a lot of positive cash flow as we invest in it. Because we own the full stack, we keep the value of every token we serve instead of renting out compute at wholesale prices.

We expect the Token Factory to unlock a new fast-growing revenue stream with meaningful higher margins, a major step in turning our infrastructure into full-scale AI business. Let's talk about the $200 million project-level debt financing. As announced on October 13, 2026, we received a commitment letter from a major lending institution for $200 million in debt financing, syndicated by Goldman Sachs to support the development of our 40 MW AI data center in Columbiana, Alabama, and to strengthen our balance sheet. The financing is expected to be structured at the project special purpose vehicle level, with an unsecured company guarantee through project completion and other limited matters.

The proceeds are intended to support completion of the Columbiana project and related project costs. Closing is currently expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to related documentation and the satisfaction of various conditions, including the lender's completion of its due diligence. 2027 outlook and capital plan. We expect to reach an annualized revenue run rate of approximately $250 million-$300 million, or approximately $21 million-$25 million per month by the end of third quarter 2027, subject to adequate financing, market condition, and various other conditions. Approximately $143 million of that run rate is supported by current operation and the Columbiana tenant agreement.

The balance is expected to come from additional AI colocation and GPU capacity currently in development and in customer negotiations. CapEx. We expect 2027 CapEx of approximately $350 million. Primarily for approximately 10 MW of AI inference or Token Factory at 85%-90% margins, capacity and the completion of our phase II Columbiana. We intend to fund this principally through customer deposits and prepayment and contract debt financing, including the proposed $200 million facility together with cash on hand. This approach ties capital deployment to contracted revenue and is designed to minimize shareholder dilution. I want to remind every shareholder that in 2016, I invested from my personal cash $8 million, and I never sold one share.

Just to tell you that I have a long-term vision of a huge return on my investment. US Data Centers update. Digi Power X owns approximately 48% of US Data Centers Inc., which design and deploys the ARMS modular AI data center system and is developing URP-1, a robotic platform for automated deployment and maintenance. USDC is raising capital independently, which will further dilute our ownership interest without capital contribution from Digi Power X, without the issuance of Digi Power X shares. In order to fund our growth, which is very promising on US Data Center, we're going to raise capital without diluting Digi Power X or without getting any allocation on Digi Power X.

I think that's very important for everyone to understand that Digi Power X today is very focused on power, on GPU bare metal, on colocation deal, and cannot afford to allocate extra dollars to expand robotics or modular systems. That's the reason why we have a different setup to raise capital. What are the opportunity for growth and expansion? We continue to prepare our New York infrastructure assets for conversion to AI data center operation, and we are targeting the transition of these sites beginning of third quarter and fourth quarter 2027. These sites are powered.

One is powered for the last 10 years, 18.7 MW, and another one where we have a total of 120 MW, including our generation of power, is being powered for 30 years in terms of generation. We got an allocation from the utility, which is great because it's all green power, hydropower, and we got an allocation of 63 MW there. Because of our financial discipline, we haven't rushed to develop it simultaneously with the Columbiana, Alabama AI Center in order to control our CapEx. We don't want to rush and be out of cash.

As we transition from a project to execution, which we have been sharing videos of our progress, and I was there actually a few days ago, and it's really, we are very close to finalize phase I, few weeks. As we transition from project to execution to live, then we can keep on going with our other assets. In North Carolina, we own now two sites, about 40 acres adjacent to one of the state's largest electrical switchyard. Our current development plans contemplate 2x 75 MW, about 150 MW for 2029 and 2030. That will secure our growth for the future years.

Between New York and North Carolina, we can expand to over 400 MW worth of capacity, which depending how we optimize each megawatt, is huge revenues. We definitely have currently, we own the assets to grow 2x, 3x every year for the next few years. Revenue increased 85% over the previous quarter, and AI now accounts for nearly half of our business, all before the expected start of Columbiana colocation billing in January 2027. Our priority now is execution, financial discipline, and then we expand our compute capacity and convert our power assets into long-term contracted revenues. We ended our quarter with approximately $120 million in cash and cash equivalents that give us a strong foundation for this next phase.

We are building this business with a clear focus on value per share. Our approach is to secure bankable customer commitments, deploy capital against attractive returns, and fund expansion through customer contribution and contract-backed financing. Our ambition is substantial, and our discipline is equally clear: grow recurring revenue and cash generation while minimizing shareholder dilution. Thank you for joining us today. We will now take questions.

Moderator: Thank you. Our first question is, what do Q3 results demonstrate about Digi Power X's AI transformation?

Michel Amar: It is really an incredible quarter for us. If you think that last year we were a basically dying Bitcoin company, and we had very little cash, January 2025, I think $1.7 million, very little assets, net fixed assets were like $30 million. And in a year, we went from no cash, little assets, a Bitcoin dying business, to cash, $130 million, $140 million of net fixed assets, CapEx this year already invested of $160 million, and AI revenues that represent almost half of our total revenue. We believe that it was a transformative year and quarter as we are growing accordingly to our pace.

We started to process data bare metal rental in May very successfully, and a lot of companies came to our site to see our execution, and everybody is very impressed.

Moderator: How much revenue is recurring or contracted?

Michel Amar: Columbiana, Alabama, provides our strongest long-term contractual revenue visibility with a 10-year take-or-pay agreement. phase I represents approximately $402 million in contractual fees, increasing to approximately $1.07 billion with phase II. NeoCloudz and our other operating business also generate ongoing revenue, although contract duration and utilization vary anywhere from two to five years. We are focused on increasing the share supported by long-term commitments, five years for NeoCloudz and 10-15 years for colocation.

Moderator: Thank you. What does the December 15 Columbiana milestone represent?

Michel Amar: December 15 is a key number, and considering that we signed the deal with our tenant, Cerebras, early May, which is really few months ago, it is really incredible that we managed to design and finance and set up phase I in basically seven months. I believe we are one of a kind to be able to execute on such a short period of time. December 15, tenants will have access to the data hall, and we will start commissioning the power and all the liquid cooling systems that are basically done. It is a very important delivery milestone for us, as a landlord, after the commissioning, we can start billing.

Moderator: Thank you. What is the financial value of the Columbiana agreement over 10 years?

Michel Amar: As stated a few minutes ago, the 15 MW first phase represents about $402 million over 10 years, and the second phase of 25 MW represents an additional, a little bit over $600 million, for a total of $1.07 billion, averaging about $107 million annually.

Moderator: Thank you. Is phase II on track for March 2027 tenant access?

Michel Amar: Construction of phase II has already started. There's a lot of common denominators between phase I and phase II. The data hall has both phases in the data hall, so it's there. All the fire suppressing requirements, all the chillers are already there for both phases, phase I, phase II. All the equipment has been purchased for both phases, phase I, phase II. We designed that contract to be able to do two phases so we can financially support it no matter what. And we are very advanced in the phase II as well. We don't see any issues to be giving access to phase II in March 2027.

The commissioning will be easier because all the liquid cooling commissioning will be done, this month and early December. We believe that the type of commissioning will be shorter in March, and we expect to bill in April the full total monthly contract.

Moderator: Thank you. What additional value could the renewal options under the Cerebras contract provide?

Michel Amar: It's a little bit under $1.1 billion for the initial term, and we can go to a total of $2.5 billion as an option. We believe that the investment of a tenant is so huge, they're going to locate in that data hall billions of U.S. dollars of equipment, of servers and GPUs, and it's very costly for a tenant to move out. Not only it's costly, it's their economic interest to stay as much as they can, as the power shells are very scarce these days. The value in our opinion will be much greater in 10 years from now.

Moderator: Thank you. Where does the proposed $200 million financing stand?

Michel Amar: It's interesting because earlier, we had an approved financing that I denied in July from one of the biggest world institutions, because I didn't like the terms. Then we decided to deny an approved financing to move and syndicate it through Goldman Sachs, which saved us on this financing about 2 points, which is incredible. As the interest rate went up, we managed to save 2 points on the financing. We are pretty close to close the financing. We got the loan documents, so we expect to close in the near future, definitely in Q4 2026, but we are pushing to close earlier.

I think we are one of the best candidates for a lender, as we invested our own capital, we have cash, and we are executing on time. We're a pretty good candidate for a lender. But we managed to be in single-digit interest, which is rare these days.

Moderator: Thank you. How will the approximately $350 million 2027 capital plan be funded while minimizing dilution?

Michel Amar: Our funding strategy combines customer deposits and prepayments. With the crisis that happened in the last four, five weeks, which was torture for our stock price, but [inaudible] company, the entire market went down. It also gave us an opportunity to ask for bigger deposits on new contracts. Now the few discussions that we have, and we're finalizing to set up new contracts, we are getting much more than we used to six months ago. If six months ago, a tenant or a bare metal renter was willing to give you 15%, now they are willing to give you 30%, and sometimes up to 50%, and sometimes, as we are negotiating now, up to 70%.

Then, financing from the customer perspective becomes so easy for us to grow because we achieved something incredible. We are credible. We are not a company that talks about power and may have a connected power with a grid in 2028, 2029. We are executing, and a lot of very big companies came to our sites, very large companies came to our sites and understand that we are for real, that we are credible. Now they are willing to support us and give us bigger deposits and help us finance our growth. That's the major accomplishment that we are realizing by execution.

Moderator: Thank you. What supports the $250 million-$300 million annualized revenue target?

Michel Amar: We already have about $143 million on the contract, and the remaining $107 million-$150 million are expected from our development of the other sites through colocation or GPU capacity. If we had an open bank checkbook, we could have done it for Q1 or Q2, but considering the market condition and our financial discipline, if we want to go fast, we have to walk slowly. We have to be careful. We survived all the Bitcoin cycle years since 2016. We always survived. We do not want to be exposed to a financial issue by growing too fast. We have time.

There is plenty of market share for us to get, and we believe that Q3 will be in the run rate of what we announced.

Moderator: Thank you. Can operations generate sustained positive cash flow?

Michel Amar: Let us talk about Q3. We generated $4.7 million of positive cash flow in Q3. True, with the help of a $12 million non-refundable tenant infrastructure contribution, and we believe that next quarter, we will also be cash flow positive between the business and additional non-refundable contribution, a bigger one this time because of the relationship from 15 MW-25 MW. Then we are live, then we have cash flow coming in. We believe we are in a good position today to create positive cash flow.

Moderator: Thank you. What drove NeoCloudz growth, and are its margins sustainable?

Michel Amar: We started with bare metal GPU rental, and you saw the increase of 127% sequentially to $2.46 million as NeoCloudz scaled. The opportunity of bare metal and GPU as a service and Token Factory is to increase your revenue per megawatt and your margins per megawatt. Considering the environment, the political environment, and by the way, we are very lucky to be in Alabama.

I was at the election night last Tuesday with the governor-elect, the coach, Tommy Tuberville, which I have a great relationship, and he reiterated directly to me that he's welcoming data centers in Alabama, and he's welcoming our contribution, he's welcoming our job creation, he's welcoming the incredible science and technology of AI that will save lives, cure cancer, and cure most of incurable diseases. So he's very pro-technology and is welcoming growth in Alabama. We're very excited because we definitely can expand in Alabama and contribute to the communities and create value to these communities by creating a lot of jobs. Now, in our campus, in a very small city, we have about 250 construction workers.

Highly paid jobs that are going to restaurants, that are going to hotels, that are creating an economic boom locally. So, it's really interesting, and we're really excited to be in Alabama there. And to go back to this business of maximizing and optimizing per megawatt, considering the scarcity of power and the upcoming regulations of power, where they're going to start to basically state-to-state limit powers below 50 MW, I don't think that you're going to see 500 MW campus or 1 GW campus. I think the strategy is more into the 50 MW, 25 MW campuses, which is very big if you do GPU bare metal. Very big revenues.

Today, bare metal, we can book short-term B300 at $775 per hour, bare metal. If we do tokens, it's $15-$20 per hour equivalent, per token. So, the pricing is booming on the GPU as a service. And it makes sense because the bottleneck, the struggle, the constraint is permitted available power. And why it creates an opportunity for a small company like ours is that we do own the power. We understand all stacks from power generation to Token Factory, which is very rare. Not a lot of companies generate power and are able to sell tokens. And every megawatt now, we know how to maximize the revenue and the value.

We can get easily $2 million-$3 million a month per megawatt. So, if I just convert 50 MW, that's $100 million a month. Okay? At very, by the way, very high margins, 85%-90% margins. Our catalyst is execution, which we are 95% there, and financial discipline, and we are an incredible company.

Moderator: Thank you. What is the path to securing an AI customer for New York?

Michel Amar: The market is such that there is so much demand, and there is much more demand today than six months ago. As we shifted from training to inference, it is exploding. The demand is exploding. We have many potential contracts now that we could sign, and we are being very, very cautious and making sure that we leverage the scarcity of our powered assets. Like New York is permitted and running Bitcoin still, legacy business, as a data center. It is there, so we just have to shift it to a redundant data center. And we want to make the right deal for the company.

We were not in a rush because of the financial discipline, and we want to close our debt financing, and then we are going to develop our New York asset, which is going to be an incredible revenue asset. And there is plenty of demand. There is no issue of finding a customer. Plenty of demand, and including few IG, investment-grade customers. We are very excited about New York.

Moderator: Thank you. How does the 48% USDC ownership create value for DGXX shareholders?

Michel Amar: The value and the protection of Digi Power capital. Of course, Digi Power would want to produce everything, transformers, switchgear, and will be without any capital left for the focus business. By being a major shareholder, the biggest shareholder of US Data Centers Inc., that is now planning to produce pod system, which are very adequate, by the way. The timing is incredible because you are going to see, we are getting on the US Data Centers Inc. a lot of action on smaller sites, because that is what is available and that is what is under the radar politically. A lot of action for us for 2027 and 2028.

It is going to be an incredible company, by the way. Related to this modular system that are housing all the different brands of GPUs, not only NVIDIA, but the B300, the Vera Rubin, the Vera, NVL4, NVL8, the Cerebras CS-4, CS-5, the AMD, the Helios, the GB300. We have everything set up. Under the US Data Centers Inc., we are also getting deposits from customers to finance the growth along with debt financing in the future. The slight dilution to get capital does not affect whatsoever Digi Power X. Now, on US Data Centers Inc., we are looking to create a nice size value for that company as we are developing as well robotics.

We actually have industrial robots that will be live this quarter, 2026, and they are going to be related to industrial sites for maintenance, variation of temperature or humidity, or all the different basic data that is needed in a data center. We are going to start to lease these robots to different industrial sites. By creating value there, Digi Power has a free take on a big piece of the value of the growth of US Data Centers Inc. without any risks that, by the way, cannot afford to take. We do not have a money allocation to go and invest in new ventures. We have to focus on our core business, on the Digi Power X, and execute.

We have a three to five-year plan that take us to a very high level, and that is what we should do.

Moderator: Thank you. What milestones should shareholders use to judge execution over the next two quarters?

Michel Amar: It is very simple. It is purely execution. phase I, tenant access in basically five weeks, four to five weeks. Commissioning starting December 15 or earlier. Billing starting January. Closing of a proposed financing in the next few weeks, but in quarter 2026. Progress of a phase II and access in March 2027. Commissioning and live and billing in April 2027. Adding few AI customers with huge deposits so we do not have to, A, dilute, and we can negotiate the best financing, debt financing, if necessary. This milestone will show how effectively we are converting our investment into recurring revenue.

Moderator: Thank you. Do you anticipate continued growth in the NeoCloudz sector going forward?

Michel Amar: We believe that this is the best use and the best ROI of our investment. Because when you work at 85%-90% margins and you have scarce power connected, this is the best use of your dollars. We do not see any slowdown in the next three to five years. We are actually negotiating contracts now, five-year contracts that are huge and with very little power, so we can execute. We see a continued growth in that sector. We just have to make sure we figure out the financing properly.

Moderator: Thank you. Our final question. How do Cerebras' Q3 results impact Digi Power X?

Michel Amar: A lot of shareholders call me and say, "But are you sure about Cerebras? Their stock was $360, it went down to $100. Aren't you worried?" I said, "How can I be worried about one alternative of NVIDIA?" Their result yesterday showed that they are doing great. They are up 55% year-over-year. Their cloud services revenue, 255%. They have close to $8 billion in cash. We have an incredible relationship with Cerebras, from management, CEO, to everyone. They are very, very happy with us. We are very happy with them. We can grow further with them. The only reason that we did not grow are for the same reasons I mentioned earlier.

We need to go step by step and be disciplined financially. As you know, they announced that they have 700 MW contracted, and 700 MW is hard to find today. They will definitely take more colocation from us, 100%. We just want to make sure that we have a diversified base of customers so we can be more valued. You have to understand one important factor. In March, when our data center is done, state-of-the-art, by the way, designed by one of the best designers in the U.S., when our data center is done, our value for liquid cooling data center today is about, in my opinion, $30 million-$35 million a megawatt of IT.

I will tell you how I base my valuation. Blackstone paid, before the election, $27 million a megawatt for a data center in West Virginia. After the election, it is worth easily 20%-30% more because of the scarcity and potential regulation in Texas and so on. A finished data center alone, the value of it, excluding the contract value, is $30 million-$35 million a megawatt. Multiply by 40, and you get an idea of what it is worth. Deduct the $200 million debt financing out of $1.2 billion or $1.4 billion, then we have a net equity there of $1.2 billion. That is what it is worth.

Add now the contracted value that brings monthly EBITDA, recurring revenues, guaranteed, and you add another $200 million there. We are very confident that our relationship with Cerebras has detonated our credibility. I believe that Cerebras GPUs are very powerful in token per second, TPS, inference. With all the trouble in NVIDIA, Cerebras is very well positioned to grow and take market share. Considering NVIDIA has 90% of market share, I would not be surprised that NVIDIA start to go down in market share and Cerebras start to grow in market share. They are going to need good partners that they trust, and we are one of them. We are very excited about our relationship with Cerebras. Any more questions?

Moderator: No, that was our final question.

Michel Amar: Okay. Thank you, guys. Thank you, shareholders, for your patience and your support. I know it gets very frustrating to go through the cycles of ups and downs on the stock price, but we are very committed. We have an incredible team. I really want to thank my team, Alec specifically, who is not a big talker, but he does a lot of work. He is the one who triggered that Cerebras deal and negotiated that Cerebras deal since last year. He has a lot of incredible deals on lap now that we are going to convert in the short term. We have a great team in West Coast.

We acquired a building, 18,000 sq ft in Sunnyvale, very close to Cerebras, very close to Supermicro, Google. Beautiful building that we are renovating and making beautiful state-of-the-art offices, where we are going to have our racks of B300, Vera, and we are going to be able to use it as a showroom and demonstration of our capabilities. We are going to have a small Token Factory there, and we are building an incredible team with Jag and his different engineers. Of course, again, we make sure to grow related to our revenue growth, as a ratio of revenues. I forgot to mention also, and I will close the statement, we lower our SG&A expenses 30% from Q2 to Q3.

We are trying to be very disciplined in how we allocate dollars. Everybody knows that we have an entrepreneurial approach to business, not a very corporate approach. I let the lawyers be corporate, the accountant be corporate, but as far as speed of execution, we are a very small team that can communicate and execute and make decisions very, very quickly, so we can compete. But we have a good shot of getting market share here. Thank you so much, everyone, and let's hope we get a great day today. Thank you, guys.

Moderator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.

#3186. Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence

After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

#3185. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

#3184. Alexander Rinke says Europe needs AI champions to share in the next wave of AI value

Alexander Rinke told the TNW Podcast that companies and public agencies want to own their AI weights. The Celonis co-founder and co-CEO also set out his test for real product-market fit.

TNW’s Cristian Dina (left) and Celonis co-CEO Alexander Rinke at HumanX in Amsterdam, 23 September 2026

Thirty years ago, Europe’s GDP was roughly on par with the US, Alexander Rinke told TNW. Today it is dramatically less. The Celonis co-founder and co-CEO does not want AI to make that gap wider.

Rinke spoke to Cristian Dina for the TNW Podcast at HumanX in Amsterdam on 23 September. Earlier that day he had joined a panel on stage called “Can Europe Actually Build Sovereign AI?”. Earlier guests include Steve Lucas of Boomi, Arvind Jain of Glean, and Daniel Dines of UiPath. The full conversation is in the video below.

Countries and groups of countries such as Europe want control over parts of the AI stack, Rinke said. They want to know where their data and their IP go. Europe also needs its own companies to take part in an AI economy that will be huge.

“We need to really foster local champions, not because we don’t trust the Americans or we think AI is going to kill us all. Just because we want to make sure we take part of the upside.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Celonis is one example, he said. Its headquarters are in New York and Munich, and it has more than 20 offices around the world, with a strong presence in Germany, Spain and the UK. Europe is “not a satellite for us,” he said.

For a company or a public agency, sovereign AI means owning its own AI, Rinke said. In the end, that means owning the model weights.

“They don’t want to give all of their data to any model to train on that data.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Every organisation is like a snowflake, he said, so its processes and their context are unique. That needs open platforms that can be installed in sovereign environments. Celonis keeps a customer’s process data with the customer and does not send it anywhere. It also helps customers tune open-source models for specific business tasks. For those tasks, he said, they can get the same or better results than with frontier models.

Rinke started Celonis 15 years ago with his co-founders, Martin Klenk and Bastian Nominacher. They first wanted to build models that could simulate how a business works. To feed a simulation, they needed to know how the business ran today, and companies could not tell them.

“So we built an x-ray machine that looks at the data the business generates and x-rays how the processes work.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Celonis now calls this process intelligence. It maps how work really gets done, across systems and outside them, so companies can redesign it with AI. The company has about 3,500 people, he said.

Celonis recently bought Ikigai Labs, an MIT spin-off. Ikigai builds specialised models for tabular and time-series data and for what-if simulation. A large language model can use them as a tool, Rinke said, for jobs such as forecasting a supply chain or deciding whether to settle an insurance claim.

Asked about an IPO or new funding, Rinke spoke about the next phase of growth instead. He pointed to the Context Model that Celonis launched and to the Ikigai deal. Celonis describes the Context Model as a living model of a business in motion, built from its operational data and connected to its strategy.

Many startup pitches claim product-market fit that the company does not have, Rinke said. His test has four questions. Is the product valuable? Is it uniquely valuable, or easy to replace? Is it repeatable, or custom each time? Will customers keep paying for it?

“It’s easy to say that you have. It’s very easy to put on a slide for VCs.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

If the answer to all four is yes, the next step is what he calls product-market-people fit: the organisation needed to scale it. Scaling too early can grow revenue that does not last, he said, especially in a boom market like AI.

Celonis was his first real venture. The founders started it during their studies, and Rinke put his master’s on hold and never finished it. They bootstrapped for five years, and winning the first enterprise clients without references was very hard, he said.

Venture capital is a good idea if a company wants to move quickly, Rinke said. But it does not replace the work a bootstrapped company has to do.

“You shouldn’t build the company to raise capital. You should build the company for customers.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

He now works much more closely with Celonis engineers than he did a few years ago. He oversees some technical projects himself and is involved in how the company adopts AI internally. Asked whether he is technical, he said: “Yeah, pretty technical.”

Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. He has interviewed 300+ industry leaders and authored the book King of Networking, establishing hi (show all) Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

#3180. Kolibri Global (KGEI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Higher oil prices lifted revenue as new wells came online later.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Kolibri Global Energy Inc. (KGEI -9.17%) reported a quarter defined by higher realized pricing and the strategic testing of new geological intervals. Management focused on the successful flowback of three Clifton Mack wells and the initial production results from the Lovina 5-8-1HF well, which represents the company's first test of the False Caney formation. While production during the quarter was affected by temporary shut-ins related to drilling activities, the company ended the period with an exit rate of approximately 5,700 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Financial performance remained stable with flat net income as increased revenue was balanced by unrealized losses on commodity hedges. Management expressed confidence in the company's debt position and current liquidity, noting that the credit facility was recently redetermined with a $75 million borrowing base.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Kolibri Global Energy's Third Quarter 2026 Financial Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded. I advise participants that this conference is being recorded today, November 13, 2026. This call will be available on the company's website at www.kolibrienergy.com. Here is a disclaimer. This call may include forward-looking information regarding Kolibri's strategic plans, anticipated production, capital expenditures, exit rates and cash flows, reserves and other estimates and forecasts. Forward-looking information is subject to risks and uncertainties, and actual results may vary from forward-looking statements.

This call may include future-oriented financial information and financial outlook information, which Kolibri discloses in order to provide readers with a more complete perspective on Kolibri's potential future operations and such information may not be appropriate for other purposes. For a description of the assumptions on which such forward-looking information is based and applicable risks and uncertainties and Kolibri's policy for updating such statements, we direct you to Kolibri's most recent annual information form and management's discussion and analysis for the period under discussion as well as Kolibri's most recent corporate presentation, all of which are available on Kolibri's website. Listeners should not place undue reliance on forward-looking information.

Kolibri takes no obligation to update any forward-looking future-oriented financial or financial outlook information other than as required by applicable law. I would now like to turn the call over to Mr. Wolf Regener, the President and CEO of Kolibri Global Energy, Inc. Please go ahead, sir.

Wolf E. Regener: Thank you, and thank you, everyone, for joining us today. With me on today's call is Gary Johnson, our Chief Financial Officer. As hopefully, everyone has seen, we released our third quarter 2026 results this morning. And if you've looked at them, then hopefully, you'll agree that it was a very solid quarter. Gary will go into the financials, but I'll speak a little bit to the operations side of things. We've accomplished quite a few things in the third quarter. In the quarter, we completed the 3 Clifton Mack wells and started flowback right at the end of the quarter.

So the production from those wells realistically started in the fourth quarter, and we'll have the benefit of that in the fourth quarter and on. Also in the third quarter, we finished drilling the Lovina 5-8-1HF well, which is our first test of the False Caney formation. This well was completed in October, and you've all hopefully seen the results we put out a few days ago about this well. We're really excited that the Lovina well is performing so well from this new interval. It's always great to have a good well, but it's even better when it's coming from a previously untested interval and it goes so well.

We'll continue to monitor the well, but it really is looking good and strong. The interval is present over most of our property. And since our reserve report includes no False Caney reserves so far, this will hopefully perform as we expect it to and then will be a material catalyst for the company and lead to meaningful increases in our reserves and in turn, value for our shareholders. With these wells coming on production, our current production rate is around 5,700 BOE a day, giving us some strong production, and that actually doesn't include a few wells that we're doing some work on right now.

Now with that, I'll turn the call over to Gary to discuss our financial results.

Gary W. Johnson: Thanks, Wolf, and thanks for everyone on the call. I'm just going to go over a few highlights of the quarter and September year-to-date results, and then we can take questions at the end. All amounts are in U.S. dollars unless otherwise stated. I'll start with the third quarter comparisons. Revenue was up 22% to $18.3 million in the third quarter of '26 due to higher prices, which were up 34%, partially offset by lower production. Average quarterly production was 3,876 BOE per day, which was down 9% compared to the prior year quarter due to shut-in wells during the quarter as well as normal decline since the new wells didn't start producing until the fourth quarter.

As we mentioned in our earnings release, our current production is approximately 5,700 BOE per day with all the new wells online. Adjusted EBITDA was $13.3 million compared to $11.1 million in the prior year quarter, which was an increase of 20% due to higher revenue, which was partly offset by an increase in operating expenses due to the increase in production and a realized loss on our commodity contracts. Our net income was flat for the third quarter at $3.6 million with basic EPS of $0.10 for both periods. This was due to the higher revenues being offset by a noncash mark-to-market adjustment of $2.4 million on our commodity contracts.

Netback from operations increased 41% to $43.48 per BOE compared to $30.84 in the prior year quarter due to the higher prices. And the netbacks, including our commodity contracts, increased 31% to $40.55 per BOE. Operating expense was $8.39 per BOE for the quarter compared to $7.37 per BOE in the prior year third quarter, which was an increase of 14%. The increase was primarily due to higher severance taxes from the higher prices, workover costs on a nonoperated well and higher chemical costs. Now I'll move on to the year-to-date September results. Revenue was up 43% to $60.4 million compared to $42.1 million in 2025 due to higher prices, which increased by 24% and higher production.

Average production was up 15% to 4,412 BOE per day for the 9 months ended September '26 compared to 3,851 in the comparable prior year period due to the wells that were drilled and completed at the end of '25. Adjusted EBITDA increased by 41% to $44.6 million compared to $31.6 million in 2025, which was due to the increase in revenues, which were partially offset by higher operating expense due to the increase in production and a realized loss on hedges. Net income was $16.1 million with basic EPS of $0.45 per share, which compares to $12.2 million and $0.34 per share last year.

The 31% increase was due to the higher revenue, partially offset by higher depreciation and operating expense from the increase in production as well as realized and unrealized losses on commodity contracts. Netback from operations increased 27% to $41.85 per BOE compared to $32.86 last year due to the higher average prices. And the netback, including commodity contracts, increased 21% to $39.79 per BOE compared to $32.91 last year. Operating expense was $8.43 per BOE for the year-to-date September compared to $7.20 in the prior year quarter. And that was due to higher severance taxes, higher prices, workover costs on a nonoperated well and also higher chemical and water hauling costs.

And like one of our shareholders have said to me [indiscernible] this is fantastic, you really hit it out of the park with it. And I said, yes, it's early days on it, but it looks really strong.

So I don't expect any negative surprises or anything. Yes, it's been great.

Steve Ferazani: Does this -- I know you've talked before this -- you drilled this well that was part of a sort of change, if not change in strategy, but just to start drilling sometimes within the other benches that you have, which could certainly drive reserves. Wolf E. Regener: Absolutely. It definitely -- it opens up this new bench in our opinion over hopefully a large section of our acreage. Steve Ferazani: Got it. That's helpful. Wolf E. Regener: Yes, I think so. I think we'll be within that range, probably a little on the lower end just because these wells came on a little bit later than we had anticipated so that affects. But we should be in that ballpark.

Steve Ferazani: Got it. Wolf E. Regener: Yes. So we like -- I mean we're going to have some good conversations with our Board as far as options that we have, right? Believe it or not, it's already November 2026. It's time once again for another weekend full of excellent streaming content that you won't want to miss. This week, HBO Max has a slate of new and new-to-the-service flicks that you should dedicate some couch time to.

First up is a sci-fi thriller from “It Follows” director David Robert Mitchell, in which an entire 1980s suburban neighborhood, Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor are yanked out of reality and dropped into a world full of dinosaurs. Yeah, we're not sure how that works either, but it sounds like a good time to us.

From there, things get a lot sillier with 2024’s notorious Spider-Man spin-off that bombed so spectacularly it’s since become a hilariously watchable, so-bad-it’s-good cult favorite, with Dakota Johnson as a paramedic who can suddenly see the future. There are plenty of unbelievable happenings in this movie, and you'll love the blissfully baffling decisions made throughout.

And then, something totally different: A 2013 documentary and one of the most beloved behind-the-scenes stories ever told, chronicling director Alejandro Jodorowsky’s wildly ambitious, ultimately doomed 1970s attempt to adapt Frank Herbert’s “Dune.” No Timothée Chalamet here.

There you have it. Clear your schedule and grab the popcorn, because these three newly added HBO Max movies are everything you need to get the party started this weekend.

What is it about? From David Robert Mitchell, the writer-director behind the cult horror hit “It Follows" comes a story about...dinosaurs? Set in a small 1982 suburb, “The End of Oak Street” follows the Platt family, headed by Denise (Anne Hathaway) and Greg (Ewan McGregor), whose ordinary neighborhood is suddenly thrown into turmoil by a mysterious cosmic event and dropped into a prehistoric world teeming with dinosaurs. Stranded in a world they don’t recognize, the family and their neighbors have to band together to survive the terrifying new dangers lurking around every corner.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Why you should watch it: Produced by J.J. Abrams, this is a Spielbergian blend of wonder and horror expertly mixed together. It's a great little thrill ride that mixes familiar “Jurassic Park”-style scares with a side of confused family, which makes for a surprisingly fun movie.

Watch "The End of Oak Street" on HBO Max now

What is it about? “Madame Web” takes a weird detour into the stranger corners of the Spider-Man universe. Dakota Johnson stars as Cassandra Webb, a New York City paramedic who, after a near-death experience, suddenly develops the power to see the future. When her visions reveal that three young women, played by Sydney Sweeney, Isabela Merced, and Celeste O’Connor, are being hunted by a mysterious, spider-powered killer (Tahar Rahim), Cassie becomes their only protector. To save them, she’ll have to understand her strange new abilities, along with the secrets of her late mother’s past.

Why you should watch it: Let’s be honest: “Madame Web” was a legendary box-office flop that critics tore apart on release. It's since become a hilarious watch even for fans of the character. But that’s exactly why you should watch it. And despite a mostly bad script and even worse acting, there are plenty of moments that will stick with you once it ends. And you'll want to make sure you're in the know for any potential future Sony/Marvel universe lore, too.

What is it about? Before Denis Villeneuve or David Lynch took a crack at Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” Chilean-French filmmaker Alejandro Jodorowsky nearly made the most audacious version of all. This documentary tells the true story of that doomed 1970s production, which Jodorowsky envisioned as a mind-expanding sci-fi epic. Through interviews with the director himself, the documentary charts how he assembled a jaw-dropping team, including artists H.R. Giger and Moebius, effects wizard Dan O’Bannon, a score by Pink Floyd, and a planned cast featuring Salvador Dalí, Orson Welles, and Mick Jagger, only to watch it collapse when no studio would finance it.

Why you should watch it: Even though his film was never made, Jodorowsky’s ideas and artwork went on to shape sci-fi landmarks like “Alien,” “Blade Runner”, and “Star Wars", making this a must-watch for fans. With “Dune: Part Three” on the horizon, there’s no better time to revisit the greatest “Dune” movie that never was.

#3177. Sierra releases Poppy 1.0 as Shopify and Meta’s Muse sign on

The standard tells AI agents what they can do at a company, and Meta's Muse now looks for it first.

More than 100 companies have now signed up as design partners for Sierra’s Personal Agent Protocol.

Sierra has released version 1.0 of Personal Agent Protocol, or Poppy, a standard for how personal AI agents deal with companies. Shopify has turned it on for every store, Meta’s Muse agent now looks for it on every site, and more than 100 companies have signed up.

Sierra has released version 1.0 of Personal Agent Protocol, or Poppy, its standard for how personal AI agents deal with companies, the startup announced on Thursday. Shopify has switched it on for every store on its platform.

Poppy lets a company tell a visiting AI agent who it is talking to and what it is allowed to do, such as check an order or book a flight. Customers sign in through standard logins and decide what their agent can access.

Meta’s Muse agent, which more than 10 million people have set up, now looks for Poppy first on every site it visits. Sierra, the AI customer service company led by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, says 60 more companies have joined, taking the total to more than 100. They include Delta Air Lines, Intuit, Salesforce and Zoom.

Shopify stores need to do nothing. Poppy handles the moment an agent arrives and identifies itself, while Shopify’s existing shopping protocol handles carts and checkout. The agent must ask the shopper before taking certain actions.

A few companies are already live. Banking firm Mercury lets agents check balances and start payments, which still go through the account’s approval rules. Turkish Airlines lets them check fares and find business-class upgrades, which customers approve before paying.

The rules are not final. Sierra calls it version 1.0, but the specification is still labelled a draft and allows changes that could break existing setups.

Sierra and Meta first unveiled Poppy in October. It is one of several efforts to set rules for AI shoppers, as Visa and Mastercard build ID checks for agents. Amazon, meanwhile, wants shoppers to use its own agent rather than Muse.
