Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

#3138. I’m Begging You, Don’t Let AI Bots Manage Your Money

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Your bank probably won't cover the mistakes you give AI permission to make.

If you’re using AI agents to manage your money, you should probably stop right now.

Agents such as Meta’s Muse, OpenClaw and OpenAI’s dots are all the rage in the AI world these days. They promise to do more than chatbots that give you information. Instead they’re tools that can take action if you ask them to.

When you first sign up for an AI agent, you may be asked to grant permission for it to access your apps, browsers and data so it can work with them. That might put your money at risk in unexpected ways.

“The intention might be something simple, like managing a calendar. But that access can give the agent the ability to do much more than the person intended,” said John Strand, the owner of the cybersecurity firm Black Hills Information Security. While you may be giving the agent access to simple smart home routines or getting help planning a trip, your banking information may also be accessible.

It might be tempting to think you can automate your financial chores and have more time for other things, but handing over your account credentials to an agent opens you up to many different things that can go wrong.

For one, AI agents might not be as secure as you think. This technology is very new — these kinds of always-on, persistent agents have really only been available for less than a year, and big companies like Meta and OpenAI have just put out their own versions in the last couple of months. These aren’t polished products that have had all the kinks worked out.

One of those challenges is that they don’t always behave in the way you expect or do what you want them to. Recent news stories about AI agents hacking other websites — including the AI platform Hugging Face and Australian government sites — have involved agents acting in unexpected ways to achieve an assigned goal. You don’t want AI to act like that with your checking account.

When agents use your login info, “a bank cannot tell an authorized agent from an attacker using the exact same login,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov. “That is more of an identity failure than an AI failure. Until agents carry verifiable identities, scoped permissions and an audit trail, blocking them is the best defensible control a bank has.”

Many banks are aware of the risks and are already cracking down on unauthorized use of agentic agents. Charles Schwab’s CEO Rick Wurster told Bloomberg that bots are taking the liberty to move clients’ money.

“I get a report on how many times we’ve blocked clients from using one of these agents in a week, and it’s in the tens and twenties — per week — that the big agents are being blocked,” Wurster said in a Bloomberg TV interview. “What that tells me is that while people love AI, they’re not willing to turn their financial accounts over to them just yet.”

But that number is likely growing, and with bots going mainstream, it could grow rapidly. More banks are taking action against bots to protect you.

More news of banks standing up against AI caught my attention when I received an email from Ally warning me that when customers use an AI service, they’re responsible for any actions that the AI takes.” Ally gave a warning that if you share your login information with a loved one, they may use that information in a way you didn’t intend — the same is true for AI.

The email goes on to warn that AI can make mistakes and misunderstand your instructions — which could be a big loss for you.

A representative for Ally said in an email to CNET that AI can create new ways to manage your finances, but Ally’s priority is to protect your accounts and personal data. Ally’s email also said that you should understand the risks that come with letting AI access your financial information.

“Not sharing Ally usernames, passwords or security codes is good practice. As the technology evolves, important questions around security, authorization, accountability and customer protection remain areas of focus across the industry,” the statement said.

A spokesperson from Wells Fargo also said in an email to CNET that Wells Fargo has already taken steps to block unauthorized agents from accessing customer accounts, too.

Some banks aren’t completely against AI, though. — they just want you to use their features and tools instead. Wurster added in his interview that he recommends for Schwab customers to use Charley, Charles Schwab’s proprietary AI tool, to gather market insights, ask about personal financial information like balances and manage everyday financial tasks like transfers and payments. These measures make it much safer, but in the meantime, it may be best to keep your banking business to yourself.

Personal finance expert Alaina Fingal broke down when you should and shouldn’t use AI for your money matters.

“AI can be a helpful tool for managing finances, but I think there’s a difference between using AI to assist with understanding money concepts and allowing AI to make financial decisions for you, Fingal said. She recommends using AI as a tool, but not as your financial advisor. You should make any final decisions yourself. Sharing your personal financial data puts you at risk for identity theft and even fraud.

As for letting AI actually access your accounts and do things on your behalf, Fingal said she’s concerned.

“I believe AI is moving incredibly quickly, and the safeguards, regulations, and accountability measures are struggling to keep up with the technology. And we’re prioritizing convenience and innovation without giving enough attention to consumer protection,” Fingal said.

If you want to check to see if bots have been meddling in your banking, look at your login history and account activity. Strand suggests looking for activity that doesn’t match your pattern — like multiple logins in a short period or access happening at the same time every day. That may not mean it’s your AI agent, but it’s worth keeping track of. If you notice anything suspicious, contact your bank immediately for assistance.

Strand also recommends enabling two-factor authentication now as a preventative step to safeguard your financial data, but it’s also a good time to reevaluate the access you’re giving AI. Strand recommends restricting which applications and sites AI agents can access.

“Check the permissions. Make sure they’re limited to what it needs to do the job you gave it, and remove anything beyond that,” he added.

If you’ve already given AI bots access to your financial data, Fingal recommends revoking access and changing the passwords that you’ve shared with any AI platform. Next, set up multifactor authentication and transaction alerts to stay alert.

Most importantly, keep an eye on your accounts. “I tell my clients to take 10 minutes each morning to review their bank transactions; that one habit can give them so much more control over their finances,” said Fingal.

Shang Saavedra, founder of personal finance platform Save My Cents, suggested you regularly revisit your AI agent’s access to apps and data and require it to ask for permission before accessing new data, apps and features.

If you decide to use AI for personal finance purposes, set limitations. “I’ve tested AI with some basic questions and basic calculations, and the information it provides is good for a beginner plan that gives you some pointers as to where to go,” said Saavedra. “I also like using AI to search for book and resource suggestions.”

But the actual handling of money? Maybe do that yourself.

#3137. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, enabling ‘dot’ agents to make purchases

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.”

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

#3136. Google’s new AI tool just proved Signal encryption really works – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With the aim of securing other vital systems, Google DeepMind plans to open-source its AlphaProof Code.

Researchers at Google DeepMind used AI to formally verify portions of Signal‘s underlying code — meaning they’ve mathematically proven that at least parts of the encrypted messaging app’s code do what they say, without errors. That’s reassuring given how many vulnerabilities AI systems have discovered in software lately, and how many people’s communications are protected by Signal’s cryptography. WhatsApp and Google Messages use the same encryption.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

DeepMind used AlphaProof Code, “a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents,” the researchers said. They added that formal verification “is the highest standard of security assurance,” but, without automation at scale like AI systems, difficult and time-consuming.

AI companies like OpenAI have been on a math-breakthrough tear as of late, in some cases solving nearly century-old math problems with AI. By computing at such vast scale, AI models can rapidly accelerate much of the manual work mathematicians do.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Using AlphaProof Code and building on earlier verification work by the Signal Foundation, DeepMind researchers divided the verification task into two camps. Humans worked with agents to identify what they needed to prove, and multiple agents running Gemini Carbon, the company’s latest model, then executed it. The agents also audited the proof and “highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human — just 1% of the codebase, a massive time savings,” the researchers wrote.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

For good measure, researchers tested AlphaProof Code’s ability to distinguish correct from flawed code by showing it two previously fixed Signal bugs, for which it produced correct proofs.

“Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth,” the researchers wrote. “It’s also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.”

Normally, researchers need to manually develop a proof to verify software, which takes much longer. That labor-intensive barrier has made formal verification a distant promised land, until now. The DeepMind team’s verification took a month to do what might normally take experts years.

DeepMind did not verify all of Signal’s code, but noted that this test is a step toward improved security infrastructure at a time when AI is disrupting the entire cybersecurity space.

Also: How to encrypt emails in Gmail, Outlook, and more

The breakthrough reiterates how deeply AI is both a massive risk for cybersecurity and an equally powerful fix. The year 2026 has been especially marked by AI-related security incidents, many of which involve agents. At the same time, companies like Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI are developing models geared specifically toward cybersecurity, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos.

Also: How to easily encrypt your files on an Android phone

DeepMind did not share any plans to release its findings as a consumer product, though the researchers are open-sourcing their code to help others with formal verification efforts. “Verifying Signal’s core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software,” DeepMind added

Thinking about a new smart TV? Give this free AI setup a try first, it could give yours an upgrade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's nothing more frustrating than a smart TV that takes forever to load an app, gets bogged down by menus or constantly recommends shows you have no interest in watching. And if your TV still has a perfectly good picture, replacing it just because the software feels outdated seems like a waste of money.

But what if you could give your existing TV a refresh without spending anything?

A free AI setup could help you clean up unnecessary apps, simplify your home screen and adjust settings that might be slowing things down. Better yet, it runs locally on your computer, so you don't need another subscription or a cloud-based AI assistant.

By using a local AI agent, you can manage a smart TV over your home network. It isn't quite as simple as installing an app, and the results will depend on your television. But if you're comfortable following a few technical steps, it could be an interesting way to get more life out of a TV you already own.

The setup uses three free tools: Ollama, Hermes Agent and an AI model from the Qwen3 family.

Ollama runs the AI model directly on your computer, while Hermes Agent acts as the assistant that carries out your instructions. Think of it this way, instead of asking a chatbot for advice and manually following its recommendations, you're asking an AI agent to inspect your TV and potentially make approved changes for you.

For example, you could ask it to identify apps you no longer use, turn off unnecessary animations that randomly come on, or help simplify your home screen. The goal is to reduce clutter and potentially improve responsiveness, although there's no guarantee that these changes will make every TV noticeably faster.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The biggest advantage is that the AI itself can operate without sending requests to a cloud service. Once the software and model have been downloaded, you can run the setup on your own hardware without paying per prompt.

Before jumping in, you'll need a computer capable of running a local AI model and a compatible smart TV connected to the same home network.

Android TV and Google TV are the most straightforward candidates for the original workflow because they support Android Debug Bridge, or ADB, which lets a computer communicate with the television.

LG TVs running webOS also have developer tools, but they use a different connection process. Samsung's mainstream smart TVs generally run Tizen, so you shouldn't follow Android TV instructions on a Samsung set.

Here's the basic process for a compatible Android TV or Google TV.

Open your TV's Settings menu and look for the device information section, usually under System or About.

Find the Android TV OS build number and select it repeatedly, typically seven times, until developer options become available.

Next, look for debugging settings. Depending on your TV's software version, you may be able to enable wireless debugging and pair your computer over Wi-Fi.

Some older televisions require a different ADB connection method, so check the instructions for your specific model before proceeding.

Open your television's network settings and locate its IP address. You'll need this so your computer knows which device to connect to.

Make sure your computer and TV are connected to the same trusted home network.

Visit Ollama's website and install the version for your computer. The original tutorial uses a model from the Qwen3 family.

For example, you can download and run Qwen3 8B by entering the following command in your computer's terminal: ollama run qwen3:8b

Keep in mind that running AI locally requires processing power and memory. If you're using an older computer, a smaller compatible model may be more practical, although its ability to follow complex instructions could be limited.

Next, install Hermes Agent and configure it to use your locally running model.

Hermes is the software that translates your requests into actions. The model decides what to do, while the agent uses the tools available on your computer to perform those tasks.

You'll also need to establish and authorize the connection between your computer and television. Simply entering the TV's IP address isn't enough on devices that require ADB pairing or other authentication.

This is where the fun begins. AI engineer and YouTube creator Fahd Mirza, who demonstrated how to use a free, locally running AI agent to manage an older smart TV, has shared a free prompt on GitHub designed to help the agent inspect and clean up an Android TV.

The prompt instructs the agent to check available memory, identify installed apps and separate them into categories based on whether they're needed.

It also asks the AI to get your permission before changing anything, disable apps rather than uninstall them and keep a record of changes so they can be reversed.

One of the more ambitious instructions asks the agent to build a simplified home screen without ads or unwanted recommendations. That's an interesting possibility, but it should be treated as an experimental request rather than a guaranteed feature. Full transparency, I wasn't able to pull that one off, but if you have tried and it worked for you, please let me know in the comments. Just start with something simple and reversible, such as asking the agent to report available memory without making any changes.

There are some important downsides. Developer settings can give software powerful access to your television, and an AI agent can make mistakes even when you've instructed it to ask permission first. Disabling the wrong system app could cause problems, while a factory reset may erase your settings and require you to sign in to your streaming services again. Not a big deal, but as someone who can never remember passwords, it's a frustration I felt was worth mentioning.

It's also worth remembering that removing apps or changing animations won't fix every performance problem. A TV with an aging processor or limited memory will still have those hardware limitations.

For most people, this isn't going to be easier than using the settings menu or connecting an inexpensive streaming stick. But if you enjoy experimenting with AI and want more control over a television you already own, it could help you get a little more mileage out of your current setup.

You can keep up with strike analytics, scores, fight cards and other details.

UFC fans are getting another way to track matches, stats and fighters on their Apple devices. On Thursday, Apple announced the addition of the sports organization to the Apple Sports app, which joins a lineup that already includes NHL, NFL, NBA, MLB, college sports, golf and other leagues. This launch comes just ahead of UFC 334 on Saturday, where the main event is Ciryl Gane versus Josh Hokit.

Fans can follow fight night match cards that show every bout, from preliminaries to the main event. Click on details for individual matches to find fighter information such as weight, height, reach and win-loss-draw records, with background colors that indicate the fighter’s country. Apple Sports is also supplying live stats during the event and an animated strike map shows where hits land as you watch in real time. Additionally, you’ll be able to keep up with the action using the Live Activities feature, which displays match info and updates across your Apple devices.

To add UFC to your dashboard, click the Home icon and tap Edit, then select UFC from the dropdown list. Your home screen will now include a feed for scheduled UFC matches, with the main event highlighted in the preview. Want it at the top? You can rearrange the order of all the leagues you’re following with a few clicks, with the option to move UFC to the top.

Apple Sports is a free app available for iPhone (with support for Apple Watch and widgets on Apple devices), originally launched in 2024. It offers features such as shareable game cards and real-time stats and game updates for football, hockey, basketball, golf, tennis, college sports and international soccer leagues.

#3130. All your Apple devices need to be patched ASAP – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security updates for iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, and Vision Pro just rolled out.

On Tuesday, Apple released security patches for iOS, iPadOS, MacOS, WatchOS, and VisionOS, which address wireless security flaws in Bluetooth pairing, AirPlay, and Messages.

According to Apple’s security notes, vulnerabilities can allow attackers to establish a Bluetooth connection without user interaction, bypass AirPlay connection rate limits, and join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Around half of these flaws were found internally by Apple, while the others were submitted by researchers.

You should update your devices now, as several generations are affected across device categories. The following software versions include patches:

Apple’s security notes list a fix for Messages to prevent attackers from remotely joining an iMessage group chat and reading its messages. According to Apple, “an authorization issue was addressed with improved validation” to fix the issue.

There was likely a flaw in Apple’s iMessage authorization logic that allowed an unauthorized user to inject themselves into a group chat roster without permission from an existing member.

Also: Your iPhone can spot scams for you with iOS 27

Another issue in Messages could allow an authorized added member to access messages within a group chat that were sent before they joined. According to Apple, the code that caused this issue has been removed.

One security fix across devices and software versions addresses an issue where a malicious actor could establish a Bluetooth connection to your device without user interaction.

Apple was not specific about which kind of Bluetooth attack this fix addresses; however, it’s reminiscent of Bluetooth Low Energy Re-Pairing vulnerabilities found earlier this year by French researchers.

This study explains how bad actors can exploit vulnerabilities in Bluetooth Low Energy pairing logic to execute one-click or zero-click impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks against unsuspecting devices, regardless of Bluetooth version or security level.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: Your favorite gadgets could expose you

The study was published in January of this year, and the researchers reported initial findings to Apple, which “[appeared] to have hardened the re-pairing logic in MacOS/iOS 26,” according to the study. It’s possible that Apple internally found another vulnerability in the same Bluetooth pairing logic, given how many devices across Bluetooth versions are affected.

According to Apple, this issue was fixed with “improved checks,” likely meaning strengthened verification steps during pairing.

Another vulnerability pertains to AirPlay, allowing an attacker within Bluetooth range or on the same network to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. This issue also affects iOS, iPadOS, MacOS, VisionOS, and WatchOS.

This vulnerability is similar to the AirBorne attack method. This report, published in 2025 by Oligo, describes how zero-click remote code execution, user-interaction bypass, denial-of-service, man-in-the-middle, and other techniques can be used to take control of a device that supports AirPlay.

However, the current security issue is likely less serious or far-reaching and was discovered internally.

For this issue, when you pair a device with an AirPlay receiver, such as an Apple TV, AirPlay-enabled TV, or Mac, it will prompt you for a security PIN to verify your device. You can only input an incorrect PIN a certain number of times before you’re denied pairing for a period of time.

Also: The new Apple TV 4K is always listening for ‘Hey Siri’

A vulnerability in this defense mechanism can allow an attacker within Bluetooth range of, or on the same network as, your device to use a brute-force attack, bypassing the mechanism that limits the number of incorrect PIN attempts, and eventually gain access to your device. There are only so many PIN combinations.

According to Apple, “a logic issue was addressed with improved state management” to fix this problem.

#3128. I found a hidden Android tool that solves all my tiny text troubles

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

When the print on your Android display is too small to read, and the pinch-to-zoom feature isn't working as expected, try this.

How many times have you been on your phone, wanted to read something (a piece of news, a website, etc.), only to find the text is too small and every effort to zoom in doesn’t work?

Also: 7 Android accessibility features that can make your life easier

This happens quite often when I’m viewing content in the Google News app — especially in the morning, when my eyes are still in “wake up” mode. It can be frustrating. And it’s not only text. Sometimes there’s an image I need to enlarge, but for whatever reason, pinch-to-zoom isn’t working on that particular screen.

Fortunately, there’s an option you can enable to ensure you can always zoom in on your Android device, no matter what’s on the screen. The option is found in Accessibility and is aptly called Magnification. With this feature enabled, you can quickly zoom in on the screen to enlarge any displayed content. It doesn’t matter what’s on the screen or what app is showing the image, page, or text — Magnification will magnify it.

This iteration of the feature has been available since Android 15. I found it by accident while poking around the Settings page. Since then, I’ve used it quite a bit, and it’s eased my morning frustration with reading news sites.

The Magnification feature is quite simple: once enabled, a magnifier shortcut appears on the screen. Tap that button, and whatever is on your screen will increase in size. It’s really that easy. One caveat: As long as the Magnification shortcut is enabled, the button remains on your screen. You can move the button up and down or to the left or right side of the display, but if you want the feature enabled, the button must remain.

The good news, however, is that the button does fade a bit, so it’s not glaring and in your face. You can still see it, but it gets just enough transparency that it doesn’t stand out all that much.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature

Open Settings by dragging the Notification Shade down twice, then tapping the gear icon (or tapping Settings in the App Drawer). Where this is located depends on the Android version you’re using and your device. For example, on my Pixel 9 Pro, it’s in Settings > Accessibility > Magnification. On a RedMagic 12 Pro, it’s in Settings > Features > Accessibility. If you don’t find it right away, open Settings and search for Magnification.

Once you’ve found the Magnification option, tap the On/Off slider until it’s in the On position, and the Magnifier button will appear on your screen. Tap the button, and whatever is on the display will enlarge enough that you shouldn’t have any trouble reading it.

Here’s a little tip: After tapping the Magnification button, whatever’s been enlarged can be scrolled vertically, but not horizontally. Fortunately, there’s a way to ensure that you can read everything on the page.

Also: I use Google Magnifier to read tiny print without my glasses

Tap the gear icon at the bottom right of the display to open the options pop-up. On this page, tap the “Magnifier size” icon that’s second from the right. This enables a movable magnifier you can place where you need it (kind of like a traditional magnifying glass). You can also change the size of the movable magnifier (by tapping one of the other “Magnifier size” buttons) as well as the size of the text when magnified (by dragging the bottom slider).

Also: RedMagic 12 Pro is the fastest Android phone I’ve ever seen

This feature has alleviated the early-morning frustration of having to squint (even with my glasses on) to read certain news sites. Give it a try and see if it doesn’t make your Android life a bit clearer.

#3125. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

#3124. How You Collaborate With AI on Creative Work Makes All the Difference

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A new study dives into the consequences of collaborating with AI on creative endeavors, and what it means for output and satisfaction at work.

Did you use AI at your job today? Maybe it helped you work faster. But too much AI may reduce both the quality of your work and your satisfaction with the job, according to a study published Nov. 10 in the PNAS Nexus science journal.

The team behind the study knew from prior research that generative AI was a mixed bag, capable of dramatically boosting productivity, but also prone to throttling creative diversity and worker satisfaction.

“The question we wanted to answer was whether these trade-offs are inevitable,” Kartik Hosanagar, a University of Pennsylvania professor of technology, digital business and marketing, and one of the study’s authors, told CNET via email. “Our research suggests they aren’t.”

AI is changing work quickly, with dizzying contradictions. Tech companies like Microsoft and Meta are spending millions on integrating AI into their business for greater efficiencies and output, while getting rid of human workers through mass buyouts and layoffs. Workers who use AI report some advantages, like saving 40 to 60 minutes a day at work, while suffering consequences like loss of confidence, loss of skills and a tougher labor market.

Teachers have also sounded the alarm, saying AI is essentially ending homework. Researchers say that if we don’t pay attention to how we collaborate with AI, we could start losing critical thinking along the way.

“Think about GPS navigation. It’s incredibly useful, but many of us have lost the ability to navigate even familiar neighborhoods without it,” Hosanagar said. “Something similar could happen with AI and cognitive skills.”

The study by Hosanagar’s team focused on the different ways we collaborate with AI on creative tasks. They found that the way we use AI — not just whether or not we use it — has a big effect on the final product and on our perception of the work.

“The future of work isn’t just about how capable AI becomes,” Hosanagar said, “but how we design the collaboration between humans and AI so as to support a broader set of goals.”

The researchers tasked 285 students, split into three groups, with writing assignments over two days. On the first day, no students used AI for writing. On the second day, each group used a different process for writing with AI.

Each of the groups used a separate “collaboration design” when working with the AI on the writing assignment. The collaboration designs represent different ways people interact with AI on the job. All three approaches delivered similar productivity benefits, but differed significantly in quality, satisfaction and creative diversity, according to Hosanagar.

In the first group, Human Confirmation, the AI planned, outlined, wrote and edited the assignment, with the humans just approving the work during each step. In the second, Human Creativity, humans did the outlining and planning, while AI did the writing and editing. In the third, Copilot, humans and AI collaborated during the entire process.

The researchers found that using AI in creative writing did not improve the quality of the work in any of the groups, but it did speed up the task.

People in the Human Confirmation produced the lowest quality and least diverse work, and participants reported feeling unsatisfied with it. But the other two groups, Human Creativity and Copilot, produced better work at the same speed, with participants reporting a more positive experience.

The study showed that the best outcomes happen when humans are actively involved in creative tasks, especially generating ideas and creating outlines, while AI assists with execution, Hosanagar said. “The goal shouldn’t be to eliminate human effort, but to direct that effort toward the parts of the process where human judgment and creativity matter most.”

It would be good to be wary, too, of the unintended consequences of people playing a smaller role in their daily work as they collaborate with AI.

“Our research also suggests that people derive satisfaction from having a meaningful creative role, not simply from producing a good final output,” Hosanagar said. “So, we should be thoughtful about what we automate.”

#3123. Need more AI in Creator Studio? Apple may charge you for it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With its new $50 AI usage packes, Apple is the latest company to introduce paid model for AI access.

There are plenty of AI subscriptions out there, but Apple’s AI features are among the few still accessible by simply purchasing a device. Now, Apple is shifting its business model by offering a one-time $50 purchase option to grant server-based AI capacity in some apps, starting with Creator Studio apps.

Apple is introducing a one-time purchase option for AI Usage Packs via app updates to Creator Studio. If you want expanded access to AI features in Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, the iWork Suite, and Logic Pro, you’ll need to pay.

Also: ChatGPT Plus vs. Google AI Pro: Two $20 plans, very different perks

The $50 fee applies to extra usage blocks and kicks in when you exceed predetermined limits in these apps. Instead of a recurring fee, Apple is hoping the one-time fee for intelligence usage packs will help the company offset some of the cost of AI. Users can buy a pack for Logic Pro now, and the other apps are expected to get it soon.

“Usage Packs may offer the option to prepay for the use of certain AI-based Services and represent the amount you have paid in advance for use of the respective Services,” according to Apple.

Apple’s one-time payment breaks away from what most companies are doing. Most companies offering AI tools try to offset the steep cost of running large language models (LLMs) by charging users for paid subscriptions. For example, Samsung is rumored to be planning such a subscription for Galaxy AI usage, including access to features that are currently free.

Also: The best tablets of 2026: Lab-tested recommendations

The Creator Studio apps are the only ones getting the Usage Packs for now. The legal terms for intelligence Usage Packs explain that these packs would be available in “AI apps,” which include not only Final Cut Pro, Compressor, Logic Pro, MainStage, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, but also Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Freeform, and other apps.

You’re not required to purchase the Usage Packs to enjoy the core functionality of the apps in the Creator Studio. However, the fact that the Usage Packs are to be applied to popular apps like Pages and Freeform begs the question of whether Apple plans to put a paywall on features that are currently free.

Some of the features for which you may be required to purchase Usage Packs once you exceed your limits include the generation of images, shapes, presentations, and presenter notes, as well as some assistant features. Usage limits reset each month.

Also: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Forget everything you knew about Amazon tablets

You can view your usage status for each of the applicable apps on your iPhone or iPad by tapping on More (or the button with three dots), then Intelligence Features, and Show Usage Status. On a Mac, it’s available by accessing Intelligence Features from the menu bar of the app you’re using, then clicking on Show Usage Status.

Intelligence usage packs expire after 12 months, but they roll over each month if left unused.

iPhone Duo has some incredible upgrades, and they shouldn't go to waste

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The iPhone Duo is easily the most impressive device Apple has made thus far, at least since the early years of the iPhone. Not only is it a whole new form factor, it includes things that you straight-up won't find on traditional iPhones. Certainly not the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

But as big a deal as the first foldable iPhone is, 2027 will mark the 20th anniversary of the very first iPhone. Rumor has it that, like the iPhone X in 2017, Apple will celebrate the milestone with an all-new iPhone design. Word has it that this so-called iPhone 20 will feature a curved glass body that makes the phone look like it's made of 100% glass.

But there's guaranteed to be a lot more to the next iPhone than just a fancy design. And if Apple has any sense it should take some of the better parts of the iPhone Duo for the iPhone 20, while also making sure to ignore other aspects of the foldable's design.

You may be thinking, "isn't the iPhone 20 supposed to have an all-glass design? How does titanium fit into it?", and you make a valid point. The titanium used on other iPhones is only present at the surface of the frame, and the internal body is made from much cheaper aluminum.

If the iPhone 20 replaces that metal frame with glass, then there's no space for titanium, right? Yes, but that hinges on the curved all-glass design rumor actually coming true. Glass is not the easiest material to work with, especially when you're trying to do new things. So there's a chance that design may not happen, and if it doesn't Apple needs to bring back that premium material to get that mix of strength and low weight.

Because, let's be honest, the anodized aluminum shell isn't really cutting it right now.

Steve Jobs may have hated the idea of using a stylus with an iPhone, but the iPhone Duo proved that their usefulness isn't just limited to iPads. Sure, the iPhone 20 won't have as much screen space as the iPhone Duo's 7.6-inch inner display, but that doesn't mean we have to be limited to finger-based control.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Offering Apple Pencil support on iPhones means you get a lot more precision control. Whether you want to draw, write, take notes, and so on. It offers a bunch more versatility to the way you control your iPhone, and in a way that's totally optional. This clearly isn't one of those early smartphones that only worked if you kept hold of a little plastic tip.

In a similar situation, Apple may have insisted that Touch ID is wholly inferior to Face ID, from a security standpoint, but it's nice to have options. The iPhone Duo shows that Apple can add the power button Touch ID to an iPhone, offering a discreet fingerprint scanner away from the front of the phone.

This shouldn't necessarily mean the loss of Face ID, as was the case with iPhone Duo. It would be nice if Apple offered both, and gave users the option of which biometric security option they prefer. Personally, I much prefer Touch ID over Face ID, but some of my colleagues would disagree.

Plus, where security is concerned, no amount of biometric security will make up for a weak passcode.

Split-screen multitasking is not an uncommon feature on modern phones, but it's been totally absent from iPhones until the launch of iPhone Duo — and that needs to change. Admittedly, split-screen multitasking is more troublesome on a phone screen, since there's less space to fit multiple windows. However, that doesn't mean it can't be useful on slab phones.

We've all experienced times when we're using our phone for something, and keep having to move back and forth between different apps. Having the option to multitask means that you could just load those two apps up side by side instead. Saving you the hassle of switching, and avoiding any awkward reloading that the apps might want to do when you return.

Another feature that's so common people don't even think about anymore is the hole punch camera. It's also something Apple seems to have deliberately avoided offering until the release of the iPhone Duo — and it's about time it came to more iPhones.

The obvious problem has always been Face ID hardware. This is why Apple had such large notches for so long, and why it later adopted the Dynamic Island. But we're getting to the stage where most of that hardware has been hidden away, and the iPhone 20 is the perfect time for Apple to push the rest of it under the screen where we can't see it.

If Apple can hide a camera under the Duo's screen, I'm sure it can hide the remainder of Face ID — even if the camera itself isn't ready to be out of sight.

One of the early iPhone 20 rumors was that it would have an uninterrupted display, thanks to the adoption of under-display tech. However, at least one recent rumor has contradicted those claims, and I hope it turns out to be correct. Apple markets the Duo's under-display camera as a "FaceTime camera," meant to be used for video calls rather than selfies. All because the camera quality is not very good compared to traditional selfie cameras.

The camera is hidden under the display by pixels that can effectively be switched off. Combined with a localized area of low pixel density, it allows light through to reach the camera. Sadly there are still obstacles in the way that interfere with that process, even if they're not as easy to see, and that affects the camera's quality. It's why under-display cameras fell out of favor in the first place.

That's fine on a foldable that already has a traditional selfie camera, and the option to shoot selfies with the main cameras. But the iPhone 20 won't have either of those things, and opting for an under-display camera is just going to mean users won't be able to take nice selfies.

We have seen an explosion of wide-shaped foldables this year, seemingly in anticipation of iPhone Fold and for the most part that design change has gone down pretty well. The shorter and wider screens are fairly comfortable to use, and there tends to be less unused space when you're watching a show or move on the foldable screen.

But we've also started seeing some phone companies produce non-foldable devices with wider screens. I've never used one, and I can't comment on how they compare to normal phone dimensions, but this trend is not something Apple should copy.

Apple isn't one for chasing trends, so this isn't likely to happen, but considering wider non-folding phones is still an unproven design, no phone company should be rushing to switch up its entire design language. Least of all a company that only releases six models each year.

The nanotexture display coating has a bunch of benefits for the iPhone Duo, ensuring a glare-free display and minimizing the look of the central crease. However, it also has the added hindrance of reducing the vividness of colors and making the screen look more washed out.

This is not something we want from the iPhone 20. There's no crease to hide, for starters, and the current anti-glare technology employed on iPhone 18 Pro Max seems to be doing a pretty good job and ensuring the screen stays readable in bright light. Which means the negatives of the nano-texture coating probably outweigh the positives. Unless Apple can solve the color issue and ensure the screen is still as durable as Ceramic Shield 2.

#3121. These 7 iPhone Duo-Ready Apps Make the Most of Apple’s New Foldable Phone

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Several creative apps are ready to take advantage of the iPhone Duo's many display configurations.

In addition to giving the iPhone line a new design, Apple’s iPhone Duo lets developers take advantage of several new modes to play with. But this early into the iPhone Duo’s general release, apps are still catching up to what Apple’s foldable phone can do.

The shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos. Some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s gotten an iPhone Duo (or it’s coming soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested.

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent.

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster.

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-size phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other.

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

#3120. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

#3119. Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

With the November Patch Tuesday rollout, you can finally customize your right-click menu in Windows 11. But don't skip these security fixes.

Windows 11 users who’ve struggled to navigate and use the right-click menu in File Explorer now finally have some relief. With the November Patch Tuesday Windows update, you’re now able to customize the menu to add and remove specific commands and apps so that only your favorites appear.

As usual, the monthly update is mandatory, which means it should automatically download and install on your PC. To check, head to Settings and select Windows Update. If the latest update — labeled “2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974)” -– pops up as installed with a pending restart, just reboot your computer. Otherwise, click the button to check for updates and allow it to download and install.

Also: You can change Windows settings directly from a search now

One caveat: Microsoft’s monthly updates fully support Windows 11 26H2 and 25H2. But support for 24H2 ended last month, at least for the Home and Pro editions. Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education will continue to get monthly security updates, though not regular non-security preview updates, while Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise and Education will receive no more updates after this month.

If you use Windows 11 Home or Pro, be sure you upgrade your system to 26H2 to continue receiving the necessary support and updates.

First and foremost in the latest update is the new customizable right-click menu.

The context-sensitive right-click menu is a handy way to quickly access key settings, features, and apps, both in File Explorer and on the desktop. But there’s always been a flaw in its basic design. The more apps you install, the more cluttered and disorganized the menu becomes. That was especially problematic in previous versions of Windows. The old-style, classic menu would grow so long that it would be difficult to navigate and let you find the item you wanted.

With Windows 11, Microsoft introduced a more modern and pared-down menu. But this version can also get crowded. Plus, it may not display every command you need, so you often have to revert to the older classic menu. You’re then stuck dealing with two separate versions of the same menu, leading to an even more confusing and cumbersome experience.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says

The ideal solution is a menu that you can customize yourself, and that’s what we now have, at least that’s what is now rolling out. Microsoft calls this one a gradual rollout, which means you may or may not get it right away.

To see if and how this is available, open File Explorer and right-click on a folder or file. If the new menu has reached your PC, you’ll see an entry for Customize menu. Select that to view all the available options for tweaking it. Alternatively, head to Settings, select Personalization, and then click the entry for Context menu.

There, you’re able to turn certain file actions on or off, such as Send to, Print, Create shortcut, Copy as path, and Rotate image. You can also choose which apps appear all the time, either in the main menu or in a submenu. Plus, additional options let you decide where certain commands and actions appear and whether you can still access the old-style menu.

Though the customizable right-click menu is the star of the update, Microsoft has added other surprises as it strives to make Windows more reliable and user-friendly.

Also gradually rolling out, Cloud rebuild is a new recovery option that lets you reinstall Windows 11 via cloud-based system images and drivers downloaded from Windows Update. This tool can help you recover Windows when it won’t load and you don’t have a USB drive or your own custom image. The downside is that your files won’t survive. But if you regularly back them up as you should, you can restore them after Windows is back in business.

To start Cloud rebuild, go to Settings, select System, click Recovery, and then select Rebuild PC. Your PC will then restart into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to kick off the cloud rebuild. If Windows can load, your computer should automatically enter WinRE mode, where you can then choose the cloud rebuild. You should need to make sure your PC is online via a wired or wireless connection.

The November update also enhances or fixes other Windows features and apps.

And that then brings us to the security fixes.

This month’s update resolves 1,094 security vulnerabilities, according to Microsoft, with 63 of them rated critical and one already exploited in the wild. That’s fewer than October’s record of 1,400 patches. But it still represents a hefty number as Microsoft and other vendors continue to rely on AI to find and fix security holes.

Also: Windows finally gets a built-in internet speed test tool – how to try it

Though labeled Moderate, the exploited flaw points to a serious spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. Here, a remote attacker who sends you a malicious email and convinces you to open it could cause Outlook to connect to a network controlled by that attacker. In this case, though, you would not receive any warning. Further, the exploit might reveal your username and password to the sender, potentially allowing them to impersonate you.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it,” Jack Bicer, Director of Vulnerability Research at patch management provider Action1, said in an advisory.

“Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” Bicer explained further. “That quiet connection can leak the user’s NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs.”

#3118. First Commonwealth: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Recurring federal energy tax credits could reduce the bank's effective tax rate by 1 to 2 percentage points annually.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, First Commonwealth (FCF +0.05%) reported core earnings per share of $0.45. For long-term investors, the bank's ability to trim deposit costs while expanding loan originations shows the underlying operational durability of its community franchise.

Management expects its deposit beta, the percentage of central bank interest rate changes passed through to depositors, to remain near historical levels of 25% on non-maturity accounts without fixed expiration dates. Paying market rates on core accounts keeps deposit levels steady while protecting net interest margin, the gap between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits.

First Commonwealth purchased over $50 million in federal renewable energy tax credits to offset tax liabilities and fund credit loss provisions. Settling into an annual rhythm of credit purchases could reduce the bank's effective tax rate by 1 to 2 percentage points.

The bank repurchased $88 million of stock during the quarter to optimize its tangible common ratio, a key measure of physical capital strength. Board authorization of an additional $25 million buyback program allows management to continue repurchasing shares from retained earnings.

Loan originations are rising across consumer and commercial categories as loan payoffs slow, driving loan volume higher. First Commonwealth relies on its regional branch footprint across Western Pennsylvania and Ohio alongside 35 fintech partnerships, or technology start-up agreements, to maintain pricing discipline and improve operating efficiency.

Long-term expansion depends on keeping loan growth in the mid-single digits while keeping loan-to-deposit ratios in the low 90% range. Management is focused on expanding technology investments, improving credit performance, and controlling expenses to build durable shareholder value.
